/guides/publish-from-blender.html:
How-to guides

Publish from Blender#

Status: verified on Blender 5.0.1 (Apple silicon), 2026-10-13 — installed as an Extension, published a textured scene from the N-panel (export → bundled verse-prepare → upload → compile → link shown and copied), the link rendered textured, and a dead server shows a plain-language error. Bake-on-publish verified 2026-10-13 on the same build (proof room, Blender Classroom, Barcelona Pavilion and Lone Monk, headless; the earlier Draft/High pipeline also in the editor).

One click in Blender's N-panel exports your scene as GLB, uploads it to a Verse server and hands back a streaming share link. The add-on is stdlib-only Python (no pip), speaks the public ingest API, and is machine-tested end to end inside a headless Blender (web/test/fix-verify-blender.mjs).

You need: Blender 4.2 or newer, and a Verse server URL (the hosted service is the default; your own deployment works identically).

1. Install the add-on#

Download#

Download verse_publish-blender-3.0.0.zip (3.0 MB) from the downloads page. It bundles verse-prepare for macOS (Apple silicon and Intel), Windows and Linux. Check it before installing:

shasum -a 256 verse_publish-blender-3.0.0.zip   # Windows: Get-FileHash verse_publish-blender-3.0.0.zip -Algorithm SHA256
# 2ff2dd7074cf3073b0e68e78af5ee2dcb6047b701824a84e8823930f0ba4f545

Then in Blender: Edit ▸ Preferences ▸ Get Extensions ▸ ⌄ (top right) ▸ Install from Disk… and pick the zip (or drag it onto the Blender window). No restart is needed. (Blender's legacy path — Add-ons ▸ Install… with the same zip, then enable "Verse Publish" — also works.)

Building from source instead: python3 integrations/blender/make_extension.py (drop the four verse-prepare binaries in integrations/bin/ first; scripts/build-plugins.sh builds every plug-in plus SHA256SUMS).

2. Point it at a server (optional)#

Edit ▸ Preferences ▸ Add-ons ▸ Verse Publish:

PreferenceWhat it does
Server URLDefaults to the hosted service. Set your own origin when you run your own server.
Account tokenOptional. With a token the published scene is account-owned — permanent, listed in /studio, and you draw from the per-token rate bucket (20 uploads/hour) instead of the shared per-IP one (6/hour). Create the token once in /studio; it is shown a single time.
Bake quality noteToggles the in-panel reminder to bake hero lightmaps at 4K. The exporter never downscales textures; the pipeline keeps up to 4096² on its hero tier, and base colour above 4096 at full detail through virtual texturing.

3. Publish#

  1. Press N in the 3D viewport and open the Verse tab.
  2. Set a scene name (defaults to the .blend file name) and, if you only want part of the scene, tick Selected objects only.
  3. Click Publish scene.

The panel walks through export → prepare → upload % → compile stage → done. The compile stage is the server's own live stage text (textures, geometry, packing), so the progress is honest. Esc or Cancel aborts at any point. When it finishes, the link is on your clipboard and the panel offers Copy link and Open in browser.

The add-on publishes a streamed scene; with Bake materials & lighting on (the default for scenes) your node materials — and at High your lighting — are baked first. To publish a small textured product in Fidelity mode, or to have the server bake the lighting, upload the exported GLB in the app and choose it on the upload screen.

Server errors (storage full, quota, rate limit, timeout) are shown verbatim — they are written to be actionable. Anything that arrives without the X-Verse-Error header came from the network edge, not the app, and the add-on retries it once on its own.

Bake materials & lighting (bake-on-publish)#

glTF carries one material model — metallic-roughness PBR with plain image textures — and no lighting. Anything richer in your scene (procedural textures, Mix/Add shader layers, node groups, colour ramps, vertex-colour masks, the Cycles lighting you tuned) is reduced by the exporter to whatever it finds on the first Principled BSDF, so it arrives flat or grey. The add-on can bake all of that in Blender, where the real shaders exist, right before the export:

Panel setting
Bake materials & lighting: Auto / On / OffAuto is on for scenes (6+ objects, 2+ lights or ≥ 3 m across) and off for a single product; the panel says in one line what it chose and why (Auto: Draft bake — 178 objects: a scene, Auto: off — a single product (1 object, 0.4 m) exports as is).
Quality: Draft / HighDraft (the default) bakes materials only and sends the lights live — seconds. High also bakes the lighting with Cycles into shared lightmap atlases.

What Draft does. Every material that is not already "Principled + image textures" is rendered to textures with Cycles: base colour (+ alpha), metallic/roughness, normal (tangent space; displacement is evaluated as bump into the normal map) and emission. The shader graph is evaluated through an emission proxy — a copy of the tree in which every BSDF is replaced by an Emission shader fed by the input of interest — so layered materials bake to exactly the mix you built. Materials that depend on UVs only are baked as one UV tile on a temporary quad (tiling floors stay tiled, nothing is unwrapped); materials using Generated/Object coordinates, procedural textures or vertex colours get a temporary VerseBake UV map (smart project, every user of the material packed into one square). Area lights, which glTF cannot carry, travel as 180° spot lights of the same peak intensity.

Draft is built to cost about as much as the export itself:

  • materials with the same node graph (Wood, Wood.001, the copies an asset-library append makes) are baked once;
  • a material is baked on one object per mesh — instances share the mesh's layout, so 300 instanced chairs are one bake, not 300;
  • texture size follows the unique surface (256 px/m), capped at 512 px: below 1024 px Verse carries a material in its atlas (fast to compile), and there normal and metallic/roughness maps are not shown, so those passes are skipped or folded into a mean value instead of baked;
  • PNGs are encoded on all cores.

What High adds. Every visible mesh gets its own evaluated mesh with a temporary VerseLightmap UV; the objects are packed into shared **4K atlas pages** at one texel density (200 px/m, scaled down evenly if the scene would need more than four pages) and each page is baked through one merged copy of its objects — one Cycles scene sync per page instead of one per object. Cycles bakes the COMBINED light (direct + indirect + emission, through your real shaders) at 64 samples on the GPU, the page is denoised (OpenImageDenoise) and goes through the scene's **view transform** (AgX / Filmic / Standard, look and exposure — what you saw in the render; a compositor's overall brightness is measured from two small renders of the camera and folded in), and each object is exported with its page's emissive-only <page>_Baked material — the shape Verse recognises as a bake and shows unlit. Cut-outs keep their holes (their alpha is baked into the same cells, on pages of their own), objects without a material get Blender's default surface, and the lights are not exported (they are in the bake). Instances of one scatter (a forest of the same tree) share one cell.

Both qualities:

  • Window glass stays live. Glass / Refraction BSDFs, Principled transmission and the classic Transparent + Glossy "architectural glass" are never baked: they travel as a transmissive Principled (KHR_materials_transmission), so the view through a window is the published scene behind it — a baked pane is a picture of its surface, and it came out dark.
  • Objects the camera never sees (Object ▸ Visibility ▸ Ray Visibility ▸ Camera off — light portals, fill cards) light the bake but are not published (Verse would draw them).
  • Big particle scatters (pebbles, grass, a forest) are merged before the export, within a 2 M-triangle budget: high-poly sources are decimated first (never below 64 triangles), then the instances are thinned evenly; up to 400 instances become one object each sharing one mesh, more are merged per grid cell. Without this the glTF exporter spent over ten minutes on Barcelona's 20,000 instances. This also applies with the bake off. VERSE_SCATTER_MTRIS changes the budget.

Nothing in your file changes. Linked library instances, collection instances and curves/text are realised as temporary local copies; materials are swapped through object-linked slots (and, on objects with modifiers, the temporary mesh's own slot, which is what the exporter reads); every UV map, image, mesh, material, helper object and the throw-away bake scenes are removed and every slot, mesh, modifier and visibility flag put back after the export — also on error or Esc. The panel shows Baking materials 12 / 48 / Baking lighting: atlas 3 / 6 (876 / 891 objects), Esc cancels between steps, and when the publish is done it shows what the bake did (lighting baked on 891 objects (6 atlases), glass live, 6 textures, 71.6 s). Scripts read the same as JSON from scene.verse_publish.bake_report, including per-phase seconds (phases).

Measured (2026-10-13, Blender 5.0.1, Apple M5 Pro, local server) — publish = click to live link (export, verse-prepare, upload, compile); ΔE2000 between the editor's Cycles render from the scene camera and the published Verse link from the same pose (mean over the frame; lower is closer), see integrations/bake-proof/:

SceneBake offDraftHigh
Blender Classroom (894 objects after instancing, 78 node materials, linked asset libraries, 0.6 M triangles)ΔE 21.5 · 6.4 sΔE 15.4 · 9.3 s (bake 2.8 s) — was ΔE 15.7 · 36 s (bake 29 s)ΔE 8.9 (median 7.0, SSIM 0.76) · 90 s (bake 66 s) — was ΔE 13.9 · 689 s (bake 656 s)
Barcelona Pavilion (sunset sky, water, glass, 20,638 particle instances = 55 M triangles of pebbles, lotus and trees)ΔE 33.8 · 23 s (compatibility mode — see below); before the scatter merge the export did not finish in 15 min, in any modeΔE 24.1 · 236 s (bake 34 s)ΔE 15.2 · 219 s (bake 37 s)
Lone Monk (1,268 meshes, 5.7 M triangles, Filmic −2 EV + an exposure compositor, grass/bush particles)ΔE 25.2 · 24 sΔE 23.8 · 45 s (bake 22 s) — was ΔE 23.8 · 2,038 s (bake 2,001 s)ΔE 20.4 (median 11.7) · 131 s (bake 96 s)

The publish times for Barcelona and Lone Monk are mostly the server's compile of millions of triangles, not the bake. Barcelona's bake-off export is published in compatibility mode because the server's output check rejects the plain export's bounds (the baked exports, whose collection instances are realised, stream); Barcelona and Lone Monk are captured with an orbit camera (compare.mjs --orbit) because the walking camera snaps to eye height. Proof images: Verse-Bake-On-Publish-Proof/blender-v2/.

Limits. Draft fixes the materials; the lighting is still Verse's own, so on a lighting-dominated frame its ΔE stays near the bake-off export — High carries the lighting. Lightmaps are diffuse pictures: reflections and anything view-dependent (Fresnel/Layer Weight mixes, glossy sheen) bake as seen along the surface normal. Materials that read per-object randomness (Object Info ▸ Random) bake one variant per mesh, and merged scatter instances share one. The compositor's glare, masks and lens effects are screen-space and are not baked (only its overall brightness is). Displaced geometry travels as the undisplaced mesh with a normal map. Glass shows what the published scene has behind it — the world sky is not exported, so a window onto it shows Verse's daylight backdrop. High holds the whole scene twice while it bakes (originals plus a merged page): peak memory was 8.8 GB for the whole Lone Monk proof run (reference render and three publishes in one Blender). Geometry-nodes meshes that drop custom UV maps fall back to their existing UVs.

The prepare step (2.3)#

Between export and upload the plug-in runs verse-prepare on the GLB: textures are right-sized to the texel density the scene can show (default 2048 px/m — one texel per screen pixel at arm's length), opaque base colour goes to JPEG 92 (everything else stays lossless), duplicate meshes are instanced and unreferenced data is dropped. The panel shows the tool's own progress and result. Prepared files may be up to 20 GB; without the tool, exports under 512 MB upload as they are (the server prepares them losslessly) and larger ones stop with the install hint. Preferences: prepare on/off, the binary path, texels per metre, lossless. Details, flags and how the binaries are bundled: verse-prepare.

What gets exported#

  • GLB, modifiers applied, +Y up.
  • Textures embedded at source resolution by the exporter; the prepare step then right-sizes them to what the scene can show (never upscaled).
  • Draco off (the server ingests raw GLBs and normalizes compressed inputs anyway).
  • Files over 100 MB use the resumable upload flow automatically, so a flaky connection resumes instead of restarting.
  • One automatic retry on transient network/edge failures; a 30-minute total budget, matching one server compile attempt (30 min; a build's whole wall clock is 45 min).

Baking tips for archviz#

Fully-baked exports (emissive lightmaps, no live lights) stream bit-faithfully: the engine's ground-truth harness measures the streamed render against Blender's own EEVEE output and gates at a 64×64 mean ΔE76 below 6 per view (web/test/fidelity.mjs). For that path to shine:

  • Bake lightmaps at 4K for hero surfaces (floors, feature walls); the compiler keeps the top 12 materials at 4096² by default (VERSE_HERO_TEXTURES, VERSE_HERO_DIM), and streams base colour larger than 4096 (8K, 16K) at full detail through virtual texturing (?vt=0 shows the old path).
  • Keep lightmaps as PNG or uncompressed in the GLB — the pipeline encodes lightmaps with UASTC in every path precisely so banding never appears.
  • Scenes with live lights still look right (the lit path is gated against EEVEE too — see Concepts), they just cannot match a bake pixel for pixel.

Headless test#

node web/test/fix-verify-blender.mjs       # spawns serve.mjs + blender --background (incl. bake-on-publish)
# editor-vs-link proof on any .blend (renders the camera, publishes off / draft / high, measures ΔE):
blender --background scene.blend --python integrations/bake-proof/blender_proof.py -- --server http://localhost:8970 --out out --tag scene
node integrations/bake-proof/compare.mjs out/scene.json

Next#

  • Share privately with tokens — client-only links.
  • Collect client review comments — pinned notes on the link you just published.
  • Embed the viewer — the same scene on your site.

Getting started — five minutes to a streaming 3D scene#

Verse Engine turns a GLB into a URL that streams in the browser — a 283 MB apartment shows its first picture in about 4 seconds over the internet, and a 30-million-triangle scan runs at over 100 fps on a laptop, because the viewer fetches a coarse version first and then only the detail the camera can see. This page is the shortest path from a file on your disk to a scene on your own site. Every step works on the dev server (node web/playground/serve.mjs, port 8080) and on the production deployment identically; HOST below stands for either.

1. Upload a model (≈ 1 minute)#

Open the app at https://HOST/app and drop a file or choose one — a .glb is the quickest (everything you can upload). The file is checked in your browser before anything is uploaded, and you confirm two things before you press Publish:

  1. What is this? — what the check found (a product, a scan, an interior, a building…) and how it will be shown: Fidelity for a textured product or scan up to about 6 m (published as itself, live in about a second — Fidelity mode), Streamed for interiors, buildings, BIM, point clouds and splats. You can correct either.
  2. How should it look? — a studio look and background for a Fidelity product, or the Lighting choice for a live-lit streamed scene: Keep as exported (the default) or Bake for me (preview or final — Bake for me).

Among the advanced options there are two ways to open a file:

OptionWhenWhat happens
Automatic (recommended)anything, up to 512 MB (20 GB when prepared by a plug-in)a Fidelity product is published as itself in about a second; anything else the server builds into a streamed scene (a minute or two for products, about twenty minutes for a large building). You watch its progress with a countdown, then walk the scene and get a link
This device onlysmall textured productsthe GLB opens whole in your browser with full PBR textures; nothing is uploaded and no link is created

If a build struggles it is retried on lighter settings by itself. A model (up to 96 MB) that still cannot be streamed is published in compatibility mode: the link works at full quality, as one larger download.

Draco-compressed, KHR-quantized and WebP/KTX2-textured files are accepted and normalized server-side. Gaussian-splat captures (.splat or 3DGS .ply) upload the same way as models: small ones load instantly in the browser, larger ones compile into a streamed .vsp and hand back a share link just like a GLB (browsers with WebGPU only; add X-Verse-Kind: splat when using the API directly).

Prefer the API? The same thing from a shell:

curl -X POST https://HOST/v1/ingest \
  -H "Content-Type: model/gltf-binary" -H "X-Verse-Name: chair" \
  --data-binary @chair.glb
# → {"job":"chair-9f3a01b2c4d5"}
curl https://HOST/v1/ingest/chair-9f3a01b2c4d5
# → {"status":"done","url":"https://HOST/?vpk=ingest/chair-9f3a01b2c4d5.vpk", …}

Full protocol, keys and quotas: Ingest API.

2. Get a share link (≈ 10 seconds)#

When the build finishes, the scene opens with its link; Share copies it:

https://HOST/app?vpk=ingest/chair-9f3a01b2c4d5.vpk

Copy it. Anyone who opens it streams the scene — no account, no install — in a current browser, on a desktop or a phone (Browser support). The ingest/<id>.vpk part is the scene id you will use everywhere else. The file is Ed25519-signed by the server; browsers verify it and the viewer's status reads "Streaming · verified".

Scenes that get an automatic walkthrough also offer Tour and Export video — a client-ready MP4/WebM flythrough of the tour, recorded and downloaded entirely in your browser (pick duration and 1080p/720p/native; nothing is uploaded).

Review workflow. Every share link doubles as a review round: the viewer offers Review once the scene is up. Your client toggles it on, clicks any spot in the scene (orbit or walk mode alike), and types a note — the comment is pinned to that exact 3D position, no account needed. When you open the same link, the numbered pins show where every note lives; sign in as the scene's owner (with your email or WhatsApp code, or a Studio token) and each pin grows Resolve and Delete — resolved pins grey out and hide behind a "show resolved" toggle. Your Studio scene cards list open/resolved counts per scene. Comments cap at 500 characters and 200 per scene; on a private scene they are visible only with the share token or your own sign-in.

Want the link to open for your client only? Sign in, flip the scene to private and mint a per-recipient share token — Share privately with tokens.

Useful URL options in the app: ?model=<glb> (classic load), ?vpk=<url> (stream), ?experience=<manifest> (see step 4), ?inspector=1 (devtools panel), ?tier=c (force the WebGL2 fallback). Look and performance knobs (?ssr, ?hdr, ?exposure, ?env, ?post, ?render=demand, …) are in Tune quality knobs.

3. Embed it with one script tag (≈ 1 minute)#

Paste this into any HTML page — a CMS block, a product page, a Notion-style embed. The host page needs no header changes: the engine runs in an iframe served from the Verse origin, which carries the cross-origin-isolation headers it needs.

<script src="https://HOST/embed.js" data-scene="chair-9f3a01b2c4d5"></script>

That is the whole integration. data-scene="<id>" resolves to ingest/<id>.vpk; data-vpk="<url>" and data-model="<glb>" are also accepted, and data-poster="poster.jpg" shows an image until the engine arrives (and if it never does — ad-blockers, offline — the poster stays).

Programmatic mount, when you want events and control:

<div id="viewer"></div>
<script src="https://HOST/embed.js"></script>
<script>
  const viewer = Verse.embed(document.getElementById("viewer"), {
    scene: "chair-9f3a01b2c4d5",
  });
  viewer.on("ready",  (d) => console.log("tier", d.tier, "first frame in", d.ttfi, "ms"));
  viewer.on("loaded", (d) => console.log(d.clusters, "clusters"));
  viewer.on("dwell",  (d) => analytics.track("3d-dwell", d.ms));
  const hit = await viewer.pick(0.5, 0.5); // what is under the centre pixel?
</script>

Every verb and event — walk(), pick(), play(), spawnProp(), setDepthOfField(), goTo(), dwell, interact, signed, … — is in the Embed SDK reference. The typed contract ships as verse-embed.d.ts.

Degradation is automatic and telemetered: browsers with WebGPU get the full picture; browsers with only WebGL2 (older iPhones, many in-app browsers) get a lighter build; anything else gets the poster and a link to open the scene in a browser. The WebGL2 build streams the same scenes, with the same studio lighting, shadows, bloom and reflection probes (screen-space and ray-traced reflections, path-traced stills and splats stay WebGPU-only). See Browser support.

4. Compose an experience (≈ 2 minutes)#

A walkthrough is more than one mesh. An experience manifest is a JSON file on the Verse origin that places extra GLBs into a base scene, sets the lighting and ambience, and names the hotspots a visitor jumps between:

{
  "name": "Showroom",
  "scene": "ingest/chair-9f3a01b2c4d5.vpk",
  "props": [{ "url": "props/lamp.glb", "position": [1.2, 0, -0.6], "yaw": 30 }],
  "ambience": { "particles": "dust@0,1.5,0*1", "audio": "wind@0,2,0" },
  "spawn": { "position": [0, 1.6, 3], "yaw": 180 },
  "hotspots": [
    { "id": "front", "label": "Front", "position": [0, 1.2, 3], "look": [0, 0.5, 0] },
    { "id": "side",  "label": "Side",  "position": [3, 1.2, 0], "look": [0, 0.5, 0] }
  ]
}

Save it as showroom.verse.json next to your assets and open

https://HOST/?experience=showroom.verse.json

The app shows a button per hotspot. In an embed, viewer.load("showroom.verse.json") does the same and viewer.goTo("side") jumps; the experience event hands you the hotspot list to build your own UI. Every key is documented in Experience manifests.

Prefer not to hand-write JSON? Open your scene with &edit=1 and the experience editor authors the manifest live: capture the spawn and hotspots from where you stand, tap surfaces to place props and ambience, add more streamed scenes at offsets (the Scenes section — an apartment plus its clubhouse in one link), record a camera tour (⏺, replayed by ?tour= or viewer.load("….tour.json") in an embed), and grab a share poster (📸) for the embed's data-poster. Download the JSON or Publish for an instant share link.

Where next#

  • Concepts — compile, stream, adapt to the device, sign: the five ideas behind everything else, in one page.
  • Help & troubleshooting — links that will not open, a browser that stopped the 3D view, slow networks, failed uploads.
  • Live examples — the real engine embedded four ways on this page: a streamed product scene, an animated GLB, an experience with hotspots, Gaussian splats — each beside its snippet.
  • New — Sign in with a one-time code · Plans and pricing · Camera paths · Host a web game · Spatial Bench · Verse Home · Floor plan to 3D home · Restyle a space, live · Tour together, live · Analytics · Embed anywhere · The <verse-viewer> element · React and Vue · Import a scan.
  • How-to guides — one task per page: Publish from Blender · Bake for me · See it in your room (View in AR) · Exteriors: sky, weather, fog, ground · Video on surfaces, sound in the room · Unity · Unreal · Share privately with tokens · Embed the viewer · Export a flythrough video · Collect client review comments · Tune quality knobs · Run your own server · Monitor production · Ask Verse, the site assistant.
  • API reference — every route with request and response examples, the error contract, rate limits.

headings.text: Streaming is a cut through a hierarchy#
Signed, and verified where it is viewed#

/concepts.html:
Start here

Concepts#

Five ideas explain everything else in these docs: scenes are compiled, compiled scenes stream, the viewer picks a tier, every scene is signed, and a scene is addressed by one id that works everywhere. This page is the mental model; the how-to guides are the hands.

Compile, don't convert#

A builder's model or a photogrammetry scan is far too heavy to send to a browser whole. Verse does not shrink it — it compiles it once, server-side, into a container built for streaming (.vpk for meshes, .vsp for Gaussian-splat captures):

  • The mesh is cut into thousands of small clusters, each simplified into a hierarchy of detail levels (coarse at the top, source detail at the bottom) with seams locked so neighbours never crack.
  • Textures are encoded for the GPU (BC7 / ASTC-class via UASTC) and sorted by importance: the materials covering the most world surface get full streamed textures — up to 4096² for a "hero" tier, and base colour above 4096 (8K, 16K) as virtual-texture pages streamed at the resolution each pixel needs — and the long tail lives on a shared 1024² preview atlas.
  • A walk-collision grid, a spawn point, an automatic ~30 s tour and a 2D floor plan are derived and written beside the file.
  • The whole thing is laid out so that the first bytes are the most useful ones: a few MB of header and coarse levels open the scene; the rest is fetched by byte range only when a camera wants it.

Compile cost is roughly 8 seconds per source MB on the production box (estimateS on the job record): a minute or two for a product, about twenty minutes for a 3-million-triangle building. Draco, KHR quantization and KTX2 inputs are normalized on the way in. Uploaded sources are deleted after compile; the compiled scene is what is kept and served. (The one exception is a model published in compatibility mode, where the uploaded GLB is the scene.)

Streaming is a cut through a hierarchy#

The viewer never downloads a scene. Every frame, a GPU pass decides which clusters — at which detail level — would project to roughly one pixel of error on this screen from this camera, and the residency loop fetches exactly those by HTTP Range request, evicting what the camera left behind. Consequences you will notice:

  • Scene size stops mattering. A 30-million-triangle scan and a chair cost the viewer about the same per frame; the metrics wall holds both above 100 fps on the same laptop.
  • Latency matters more than bandwidth. Refinement is a chain of small range requests, so a far-away viewer is RTT-bound. That is why an edge cache near the viewer (see the cache headers in the API reference) roughly halves time-to-sharp, and why private scenes — which never touch a CDN — are slower for remote reviewers by design.
  • First seconds are tuned deliberately. Coarse clusters carry a baked flat colour, so the opening frames read as a soft clay model with correct colours while textures arrive, instead of shattered glass. The ?vgflat knob exposes it.
  • Streaming is observable. progress events report drawn/total clusters; the ?inspector=1 panel shows residency per level; the stats channel carries everything else.

Gaussian splats stream the same way at the chunk level (.vsp: full and coarse subsets per chunk, chosen by projected size).

Tiers: what each device gets#

The viewer classifies the device once at boot and the whole stack adapts:

TierBackendWhereWhat changes
AWebGPU, desktop-class GPUlaptops, desktops, high-end tabletseverything: SSR, reflection probes, HDR output, 4K hero textures, full post chain
BWebGPU, mobile-class GPUphones, mid tabletssmaller texture pools, lean post chain (no DoF/bloom), no SSR, no hero pool
CWebGL2in-app browsers, older devicesa separate bundle, held to its own golden images on every release, that renders classic scenes and opens streamed scenes with a CPU-selected cut (compared against tier A per scene by fix-verify-tierc-stream); studio lighting, contact shadow, bloom, optional SSAO, per-room reflection probes and real-time GI; no SSR, ray-traced reflections, TSR or path-traced stills; splats need WebGPU

Dynamic resolution scaling keeps frame time inside the display's budget on every tier, and on-demand rendering parks the loop when nothing changes (the default in embeds and on battery). The embed SDK reports the tier in its ready event and a degraded event when it had to step down; the final rung is a poster image with a link out, so an embed never shows a blank box. The matrix of browsers and WebViews is in Browser support.

Fidelity: two paths#

Verse is measured against ground truth, not eyeballed. (This section is about how faithfully streamed scenes reproduce their source. **Fidelity mode** — a textured product or scan published as itself, at source resolution, with no streaming — is a different thing: Fidelity mode.)

  • Baked scenes (archviz exports whose lighting is already in emissive lightmaps) must reproduce the bake bit-faithfully: unlit materials bypass tone mapping, post effects that would alter a bake are suppressed, and lightmaps are never encoded with a banding codec. The harness renders the source bake in Blender EEVEE and gates the streamed result at a 64×64 mean ΔE76 below 6 per view (web/test/fidelity.mjs); our apartment scenes measure 0.6–2.5.
  • Lit scenes (plain PBR with live lights) are compared with EEVEE given the same scene, sun and environment through the engine's own display transform; gate ΔE below 9 (web/test/fidelity-lit.mjs). At the last audit ten of eleven reference views measured 0.5–8.2; one view of a scratched-metal helmet sits at 12 and is open work.

Screen-space reflections, HDR output and the vertex-tangent path are each gated separately so they can never drift the fidelity numbers; the quality knobs let you turn each one on or off per link.

Signed, and verified where it is viewed#

Every compiled file is signed Ed25519 by the server that compiled it (a descriptor in the header and a trailer after the directory for .vpk; an 80-byte trailer for .vsp). The browser fetches the origin's public key (GET /v1/pubkey) and verifies with WebCrypto from the bytes it already holds, then reports signed: true | false | "unverified" on the status line and in the SDK's signed event. The trust anchor is the page embedding the scene, not the host serving the bytes — so a CDN, a mirror or a copied file can never make a tampered scene verify, and a missing signature never blocks loading. (The container's byte layout is an in-repo document for the team; it is not published here.)

One id, four surfaces#

A finished compile returns a scene id — the ingest/<id>.vpk part of its share link — and that id is the handle everywhere:

SurfaceHow the id is used
Share linkhttps://HOST/?vpk=ingest/<id>.vpk — opens the playground viewer; &share=<token> for a private scene; &tour=, &experience= compose more
Embed<script src="https://HOST/embed.js" data-scene="<id>"> or Verse.embed(el, { scene: "<id>" })
API/v1/scenes/<id>/… (ownership, visibility, share tokens, stats), /v1/review/<id> (pinned comments), GET /v1/ingest/<id> while the job record lives
Studiothe scene card at /studio — poster, link, embed snippet, analytics, visibility and share links

Ownership is the one thing layered on top: scenes uploaded anonymously are retained best-effort under a disk budget; scenes uploaded with (or claimed by) an account are permanent, can be made private, and roll up analytics. Accounts are token-only — the token is the credential, like an API key.

Where the pieces run#

your page / Blender / Unity / Unreal / curl
        │  HTTPS (plain JSON + raw bytes)
        ▼
 one Node service ── ingest API, signing, share links, review, rooms, telemetry, docs
        │  spawns             │  serves by byte range
   verse-compile          ingest/<id>.vpk  ──►  (optional CDN edge)
   (native Rust)                                      │
                                                      ▼
                                browser: main thread (UI only)
                                  ├─ sim worker  (camera, walk, collision)   ─┐ shared-memory
                                  └─ render worker (Rust→wasm, WebGPU/WebGL2) ─┘ triple buffer

The browser's main thread never renders (design law #1): the engine lives in a render worker, the simulation in another, and they exchange frames through a lock-free triple buffer in shared memory. That is why the page stays responsive under the heaviest scene, and why the server must send the cross-origin-isolation headers the engine iframe carries for you.

Next#

  • Getting started — five minutes to a streaming scene.
  • Help & troubleshooting — when a link, an upload or a live tour does not behave.
  • Glossary — the words (cluster, DAG, tier, VG, residency…).

Latency matters more than bandwidth. Refinement is a chain of small range requests, so a far-away viewer is RTT-bound. That is why an edge cache near the viewer (see the cache headers in the API reference) roughly halves time-to-sharp, and why private scenes — which never touch a CDN — are slower for remote reviewers by design.
First seconds are tuned deliberately. Coarse clusters carry a baked flat colour, so the opening frames read as a soft clay model with correct colours while textures arrive, instead of shattered glass. The ?vgflat knob exposes it.
Streaming is observable. progress events report drawn/total clusters; the ?inspector=1 panel shows residency per level; the stats channel carries everything else.

Gaussian splats stream the same way at the chunk level (.vsp: full and coarse subsets per chunk, chosen by projected size).

Tiers: what each device gets#

The viewer classifies the device once at boot and the whole stack adapts:

Tier	Backend	Where	What changes
A	WebGPU, desktop-class GPU	laptops, desktops, high-end tablets	everything: SSR, reflection probes, HDR output, 4K hero textures, full post chain
B	WebGPU, mobile-class GPU	phones, mid tablets	smaller texture pools, lean post chain (no DoF/bloom), no SSR, no hero pool
C	WebGL2	in-app browsers, older devices	a separate bundle, held to its own golden images on every release, that renders classic scenes and opens streamed scenes with a CPU-selected cut (compared against tier A per scene by fix-verify-tierc-stream); studio lighting, contact shadow, bloom, optional SSAO, per-room reflection probes and real-time GI; no SSR, ray-traced reflections, TSR or path-traced stills; splats need WebGPU

Dynamic resolution scaling keeps frame time inside the display's budget on every tier, and on-demand rendering parks the loop when nothing changes (the default in embeds and on battery). The embed SDK reports the tier in its ready event and a degraded event when it had to step down; the final rung is a poster image with a link out, so an embed never shows a blank box. The matrix of browsers and WebViews is in Browser support.

Fidelity: two paths#

Verse is measured against ground truth, not eyeballed. (This section is about how faithfully streamed scenes reproduce their source. **Fidelity mode** — a textured product or scan published as itself, at source resolution, with no streaming — is a different thing: Fidelity mode.)

Baked scenes (archviz exports whose lighting is already in emissive lightmaps) must reproduce the bake bit-faithfully: unlit materials bypass tone mapping, post effects that would alter a bake are suppressed, and lightmaps are never encoded with a banding codec. The harness renders the source bake in Blender EEVEE and gates the streamed result at a 64×64 mean ΔE76 below 6 per view (web/test/fidelity.mjs); our apartment scenes measure 0.6–2.5.
Lit scenes (plain PBR with live lights) are compared with EEVEE given the same scene, sun and environment through the engine's own display transform; gate ΔE below 9 (web/test/fidelity-lit.mjs). At the last audit ten of eleven reference views measured 0.5–8.2; one view of a scratched-metal helmet sits at 12 and is open work.

Screen-space reflections, HDR output and the vertex-tangent path are each gated separately so they can never drift the fidelity numbers; the quality knobs let you turn each one on or off per link.

Signed, and verified where it is viewed#

Every compiled file is signed Ed25519 by the server that compiled it (a descriptor in the header and a trailer after the directory for .vpk; an 80-byte trailer for .vsp). The browser fetches the origin's public key (GET /v1/pubkey) and verifies with WebCrypto from the bytes it already holds, then reports signed: true | false | "unverified" on the status line and in the SDK's signed event. The trust anchor is the page embedding the scene, not the host serving the bytes — so a CDN, a mirror or a copied file can never make a tampered scene verify, and a missing signature never blocks loading. (The container's byte layout is an in-repo document for the team; it is not published here.)

One id, four surfaces#

A finished compile returns a scene id — the ingest/<id>.vpk part of its share link — and that id is the handle everywhere:

Surface	How the id is used
Share link	https://HOST/?vpk=ingest/<id>.vpk — opens the playground viewer; &share=<token> for a private scene; &tour=, &experience= compose more
Embed	<script src="https://HOST/embed.js" data-scene="<id>"> or Verse.embed(el, { scene: "<id>" })
API	/v1/scenes/<id>/… (ownership, visibility, share tokens, stats), /v1/review/<id> (pinned comments), GET /v1/ingest/<id> while the job record lives
Studio	the scene card at /studio — poster, link, embed snippet, analytics, visibility and share links

Ownership is the one thing layered on top: scenes uploaded anonymously are retained best-effort under a disk budget; scenes uploaded with (or claimed by) an account are permanent, can be made private, and roll up analytics. Accounts are token-only — the token is the credential, like an API key.

Where the pieces run#
Copy
your page / Blender / Unity / Unreal / curl
        │  HTTPS (plain JSON + raw bytes)
        ▼
 one Node service ── ingest API, signing, share links, review, rooms, telemetry, docs
        │  spawns             │  serves by byte range
   verse-compile          ingest/<id>.vpk  ──►  (optional CDN edge)
   (native Rust)                                      │
                                                      ▼
                                browser: main thread (UI only)
                                  ├─ sim worker  (camera, walk, collision)   ─┐ shared-memory
                                  └─ render worker (Rust→wasm, WebGPU/WebGL2) ─┘ triple buffer

The browser's main thread never renders (design law #1): the engine lives in a render worker, the simulation in another, and they exchange frames through a lock-free triple buffer in shared memory. That is why the page stays responsive under the heaviest scene, and why the server must send the cross-origin-isolation headers the engine iframe carries for you.

Next#
Getting started — five minutes to a streaming scene.
Help & troubleshooting — when a link, an upload or a live tour does not behave.
Glossary — the words (cluster, DAG, tier, VG, residency…).

/guides/what-you-can-upload.html:
How-to guides

What you can upload#

Everything on this page is also shown in the app's upload screen, which reads the numbers live from GET /v1/limits — so what you see there is always what this server actually enforces. The app checks your file **before any bytes are sent, tells you in plain language what it found and what it will do with it**, and lets you correct it with one tap.

Two roads#

Every upload takes one of two roads. The app decides, says so, and you can override it (Fidelity mode has the rules in full):

FidelityStreamed
Fora product, a scan — one object or a small setan interior, a building, a city — anything large
What is publishedthe file itself: Draco decoded, every texture at its source resolution and formata streamed scene: coarse-to-fine geometry and textures that arrive as the camera needs them
How longsecondsabout 8 seconds per MB of source (the app's estimate is calibrated against this server)
How it looksexactly as exported — the Khronos PBR materials, your textures, studio lighting; measured against the Khronos sample models and a reference rendererthe same materials through the compiler's atlas and streams; walkable from the first second
Rules≤ 6 m across, ≤ 10 M triangles, ≤ 48 textures, ≤ 4 GB decoded (fifteen 8K maps), textured, not lightmap-baked, not IFC/USDeverything else
Link/view?glb=ingest/<id>.fidelity.glb/view?vpk=ingest/<id>.vpk

A textureless low-poly object streams by default (nothing to keep exact, and it builds in seconds) — the app offers Fidelity for it anyway.

Formats#

FormatNotes
GLB (binary glTF 2.0)the recommended format — one self-contained file
glTF 2.0 JSON (.gltf)a fully embedded .gltf (data: URIs) on its own; a .gltf with a separate .bin and texture files: zip the folder (a model library's "glTF Separate" download as it comes) and upload the .zip — it is packed into one GLB on our side. A texture missing from the zip is named in the result and that surface shows its plain colour; a missing .bin is refused
Phone video of a room (.mp4, .mov, .webm, .avi) or a zip of room photosVerse Capture: a walkable 3D room built from your footage (beta; available where the capture service is on)
3D Gaussian-splat .plybinary little-endian 3DGS export (INRIA and most capture apps) — streamed
.splatantimatter15 raw splat records — streamed
Point clouds (.ply xyz, .las/.laz, .e57, .xyz/.pts text)laser scans and dense clouds, streamed coarse-to-fine as point discs. A text cloud is one point per line: x y z, optionally intensity, colour (0–255 or 0–1) and normal
PLY mesh (.ply with faces)a scan app's mesh export (vertex colours) — converted on our side and cleaned as a scan. Send X-Verse-Kind: cloud to show its vertices as a point cloud instead
Matterport MatterPak (.zip)the bundle exactly as Matterport delivers it — see Scans
IFC (.ifc, IFC2x3 / IFC4)BIM models — converted on our side and streamed; every product becomes a clickable object with its name, type, storey and property sets (guide)
USD (.usdz, .usd, .usda, .usdc)one self-contained file — Mesh prims with MaterialX (OpenPBR / standard_surface) or UsdPreviewSurface materials, textures from inside a .usdz; Z-up stages and metersPerUnit are normalised; references to other files are not followed (guide)
FBX (.fbx, binary or ASCII, FBX 2011–2020 / 7.1–7.7)converted on our side to glTF, then published like a GLB (Fidelity or streamed). Materials (Phong, 3ds Max Physical, Stingray PBS), embedded textures, units and up-axis from the file, animation and skins come across. Textures kept as separate files: upload a .zip with the texture folder (guide)
OBJ + MTL (.obj)converted on our side. Zip the .obj with its .mtl and textures — an .obj alone has plain colours. OBJ has no units: a model wider than 1,000 units is read as centimetres (X-Verse-Units overrides) (guide)
STL (.stl, binary or ASCII)converted on our side. STL carries shape only — no colours, textures or units — so it is shown in a neutral material and read as millimetres (the 3D-printing default; a model under 2 units across is read as metres). X-Verse-Units overrides
.zipa .gltf with its .bin and textures, or a zipped .glb (packed into one GLB); or an .fbx or .obj with its .mtl and texture folder (converted). Other scene files in the zip are ignored. A Matterport MatterPak zip is recognised as one

.blend, .max, .skp and other application files need exporting first: FBX or, best, glTF Binary (.glb) (in Blender: File → Export → glTF 2.0).

Scans#

Room and property captures from a phone or a Matterport camera are a first-class upload. Verse recognises a capture: the exporter names a capture app, the upload is a MatterPak or a PLY mesh, or every material is a single photo texture and nothing else. It then **cleans it before publishing**, in about a second:

  • Levels the floor and puts it at height 0. It finds the lowest large level surface and rotates it exactly level. Bumps of up to 2.5 cm in it (the "wobbly floor" of a LiDAR mesh) are flattened. Phone captures are usually a fraction of a degree off; up to 45° is corrected.
  • Removes floating debris. Crumbs and small fragments hanging in the air go. Anything touching the room stays, like a chair on the floor.
  • Fills small holes. A hole up to 1.2 m round is filled with texture from around it. Windows, doorways and unscanned rooms stay open.
  • Evens out the light baked into the texture. Dark corners are lifted and hot spots by a window are softened. Colours and the overall brightness are kept: the correction is gentle and never more than ×1.5 / ÷1.5.

The upload screen offers Clean up the scan, on by default; turn it off to publish the capture exactly as exported. Through the API, send X-Verse-Scan: off (or clean to clean a file Verse did not recognise as a capture). The share link's record lists what was done, for example "levelled the floor (it was 0.56° off), removed 119 floating fragments, filled 23 small holes". A scan that fits the product limits (≤ 6 m, ≤ 2 M triangles) opens in Fidelity; a larger one (a corridor, a whole floor, a house) is cleaned and streamed.

What to export, per app#

AppExportNotes
PolycamGLB (best), or OBJ (zip it with its .mtl and textures), or USDZ. Point clouds: PLY / XYZ / LAS. Gaussian splats: PLYPolycam's free plan limits some export formats.
ScaniverseGLB (best), OBJ (zip) or USDZ. Point clouds: PLY / LAS. Splats: PLYScaniverse's SPZ splat format is not read yet; export splats as PLY.
3D Scanner AppGLB (best), OBJ (zip), USDZ, PLY mesh, or PLY / XYZ / LAS points
iPhone (RoomPlan, Reality Composer, Object Capture)USDZA USDZ that is a capture is cleaned as a scan, not treated as a BIM model.
Matterportthe MatterPak Bundle (.zip), uploaded unchangedSee below. No Matterport login, API key or account link is needed: Verse only reads the file you download.
Photogrammetry (RealityCapture, Metashape, Luma…)GLB, or OBJ (zip)

Matterport: which export to ask for#

In Matterport Cloud, open the space and buy or download the **MatterPak™ Bundle** add-on. It is a paid add-on per space, and Matterport decides which spaces offer it. Upload the .zip as it arrives. Verse looks inside:

  • The textured mesh (<model id>.obj + .mtl + its texture JPGs) is the scene. Matterport writes it Z-up in metres; Verse reads it that way, then cleans it as a scan. A home is usually larger than the Fidelity limits, so it streams.
  • cloud.xyz (a colourised point cloud) is skipped when the zip is converted as a mesh. To get the point-cloud view instead, upload the same zip with X-Verse-Kind: cloud (or as a separate upload).
  • The colour plan and ceiling plan images (colorplan_*.jpg, PDF) are listed in the record but not used. Verse draws its own floor plan from the mesh.

Limits of a MatterPak to know about:

  • Its mesh is Matterport's own simplified reconstruction, with textures of about 2K each. It is not the detail of the 360° panoramas in the Matterport tour, and the panoramas are not in the bundle.
  • Spaces captured before December 2017 carry only the OBJ.
  • cloud.xyz is a reduced-density cloud. For survey-grade density, buy the separate E57 add-on and upload the .e57 directly (a point cloud).
  • A large home's bundle can pass the 512 MB upload limit, usually because of cloud.xyz. Remove it from the zip, or upload the mesh and the cloud separately.

Limits#

These are enforced. A file over a limit is refused before it uploads.

LimitValue
File size512 MB; up to 20 GB for a file prepared with verse-prepare (the Blender, Unreal and Unity plug-ins do this) and sent through the resumable upload. The glTF container itself caps one .glb at 4 GB; past that, split the export or instance repeated geometry
Triangles (streamed)no fixed cap: past 12 M source triangles the build runs region by region in bounded memory (a 1 B-triangle instanced city compiles at a 5 GB peak). The file's 32-bit offsets cap it at 4 GB: about 28 B per unique triangle plus ~2 B per repeated triangle (repeated meshes, 8+ copies, are stored once but each copy keeps its directory entries) — roughly 140 M unique triangles with nothing repeated, or ~50 M unique beside ~1 B repeated
Build time (streamed)45 minutes in total; each attempt up to 30 minutes (an attempt with no progress for 10 minutes is stopped and retried on lighter settings)
Fidelity file size512 MB (the upload cap). Over 24 MB the textures stream — a small first view in seconds, then every texture sharpened once to what the device holds; over 1.5 M triangles phones get a simplified mesh, desktops the full one (Fidelity mode)
Single-room interiors in Fidelitya one-storey room under 100 MB, 2 M triangles and 128 textures streams for phones and opens as itself on desktops from the same link (Fidelity mode)
Splat captures4,000,000 splats
Uploads6 per hour anonymously, 20 per hour signed in
Builds at once2 per server — the rest wait in a queue, and the app shows your place in it

Recommendations (streamed)#

These are recommendations, not limits — larger scenes are attempted, and heal themselves onto lighter settings when they need to.

For a quick, reliable buildStay around
Trianglesup to about 3 million
Texturesup to about 400
Texture size2K (2048 px)
File sizeup to about 170 MB

The basis is the largest scene we test on every release: 3.1 M triangles, 399 textures, 167 MB — about 20 minutes to build on the production server.

Textures larger than 2048 px are resampled to 2048 px for streaming (the 12 most prominent materials keep 4096 px). A base-colour texture larger than 4096 px (8K, 16K) keeps its full detail: it is cut into pages and the viewer streams only the pages in view (virtual texturing; ?vt=0 shows the old path). Other maps above 2K only make the upload and the build longer. **In Fidelity mode nothing is resampled**: a 4096² map is shown at 4096².

Baked in Blender (bake to emission). If you baked your lighting into images and plugged them into each material's Emission socket — the common archviz workflow, with the Base Color socket often still holding the original albedo texture — the scene is recognised as baked (and streams): every material whose emission image is a lit picture (bright over most of its texels) is shown exactly as that picture, unlit, and its base-colour texture is set aside (it is not downloaded). Cut-out materials keep their holes: the alpha of the base texture still applies to plants and grilles in Alpha Clip or Alpha Blend mode. A material whose emission image is mostly black with a few glowing texels — a screen, a lamp — stays a lit material and is listed in the Lights panel. Naming the baked materials …_Baked (what Blender's bake add-ons do) is a helpful hint, used to pick the right UV map when the bake sits on its own lightmap UVs, but it is not required and does not by itself make a material baked: the pixels decide.

Logos, stickers and posters. A flat image with transparent parts — a company logo on a wall, a sticker, a framed poster with a transparent border, a sign — is a decal: a plane whose base-colour image carries the cut-out in its alpha channel (a PNG on a transparent background). Export it in either Alpha Clip (MASK) or Alpha Blend (BLEND) mode; both work the same way. The image's alpha decides: where it is transparent the wall behind shows through, where it is opaque the picture shows, lit like the surface it sits on, and from both sides if the material is double-sided. Keep the image's transparent pixels truly transparent (alpha 0) — their colour does not matter. What counts as glass instead: an Alpha Blend material whose transparency is partial — a window pane with its alpha factor below 1 and no image, or an image whose alpha is a soft, mid-range tint everywhere (a privacy film) — and any material carrying KHR_materials_transmission. Those refract and transmit; a logo never does.

Compression#

Supported — decoded on our sideNot supported
Draco geometry (KHR_draco_mesh_compression)AVIF textures
meshopt geometry (EXT_meshopt_compression, KHR_meshopt_compression — gltfpack -c / -cc)
Quantized meshes (KHR_mesh_quantization)
WebP textures (EXT_texture_webp)
KTX2 / Basis textures (KHR_texture_basisu)

What is rendered#

Every Khronos material renders, on WebGPU and on WebGL2 (iPhones, in-app browsers), in Fidelity mode and in streamed scenes:

  • The metallic-roughness model: base colour, metalness, roughness, normal, occlusion and emissive maps, vertex colours, alpha mask and blend, and double-sided materials.
  • KHR_materials_clearcoat, with its clearcoat, roughness and normal textures.
  • KHR_materials_sheen, with colour and roughness textures.
  • KHR_materials_specular, with specular and colour textures.
  • KHR_materials_transmission, with its texture: glass that refracts and takes its base colour.
  • KHR_materials_volume, with the thickness texture and absorption colour.
  • KHR_materials_ior, which also changes how much a non-glass surface reflects.
  • KHR_materials_iridescence: thin film, with the strength and thickness textures.
  • KHR_materials_anisotropy: brushed metal, with strength, rotation and the direction texture.
  • KHR_materials_dispersion: rainbow edges in glass.
  • KHR_materials_emissive_strength, KHR_materials_unlit, and KHR_materials_variants (the default variant).
  • KHR_texture_transform on every texture: each map can tile, rotate or offset on its own, and a second UV set works too, for example ambient occlusion on TEXCOORD_1. The texture's wrap mode (repeat, clamp, mirror) is honoured.

Fidelity mode also renders punctual lights, node animation, skins and morph targets.

These limits remain:

  • Phones. The extension textures are smaller on phones (512 px; 256 px for anisotropy and clearcoat-normal maps), at most 24 MB per scene. Past that a material keeps its factors.
  • Streamed scenes carry the extension textures at up to 512 px, and anisotropy there follows the surface's UV direction (a .vpk has no tangents).
  • Not in streamed scenes yet: specular-glossiness.

The full table, per backend, is in the Fidelity mode guide. If your file lists such an extension as required, the server relaxes that requirement and builds the scene anyway; the result notes what was skipped.

Animated models#

Node animation (doors, fans, turntables — anything a clip moves as a whole) and skinned meshes (rigged figures) play in the streamed scene, at any file size, on every device; the first clip plays on open and the clip bar switches, pauses and scrubs. In Fidelity mode everything plays, morph targets included. Not carried by the streamed path: morph targets (blend shapes), and skins with more than 256 joints — a model that needs those is published in compatibility mode (the whole model as one download) so it still plays, as long as the file is under about 96 MB.

Who can open the link#

Anyone with a current browser. Browsers with WebGPU — Chrome, Edge, Safari 26, Firefox on Windows and macOS — get the full picture. Others (older iPhones and iPads, many in-app browsers) get a WebGL2 build that streams the same scene, with walk, tour, review pins and video export, and the same studio lighting, sun and contact shadows, bloom, optional ambient occlusion, per-room reflection probes, real-time GI and uploaded HDR backgrounds. Still WebGPU-only: path-traced stills, screen-space and ray-traced reflections, temporal upscaling, HDR display output and Gaussian-splat captures. The full table is in Browser support.

What the preflight checks#

Before uploading, the app reads only the head of your file and reports:

  • Red — blocks the upload: over the size limit; not a format we read; a model that references files that were not uploaded; no meshes; lines or points instead of triangles; a compression we cannot decode; a damaged or truncated file.
  • Amber — you can continue: more triangles or textures than we recommend; textures larger than 2K; a build likely to be long; a material feature that will be skipped; animations on a model too large for compatibility mode (it is built static).
  • Green: what it found — meshes, triangles, textures, animations that will play — and how long the build should take.
  • What is this? the classification (product / scan / interior / building / BIM / point cloud), its evidence, and the road it will take — correctable with one tap.
  • How should it look? a studio preset and background for a product; the Lighting choice for a scene.

The server runs the same checks — and the same classifier — again on the bytes that arrive, so API and exporter uploads get the same answers (see the API reference).

While it builds#

  • Time left is a real countdown ("About 6 min left"). It never counts up; if a build overruns its estimate the app says so. A Fidelity upload is live in seconds and the app says so.
  • If a build struggles, it heals itself. A build that runs out of memory or time is retried automatically — up to three attempts — with lighter texture settings. You will see a note such as "rebuilding with lighter texture settings — no action needed". Nothing else about the scene changes.
  • You always get a working link. Every finished scene is checked before it goes live. If a build cannot be made to work even with the lightest settings, we publish your model in compatibility mode instead: the same model at full quality as one larger download (for models up to about 96 MB). The app tells you when that happened.
  • A dropped connection is not an error. Uploads resume by themselves from where they stopped — through Wi-Fi drops and server restarts. You will see "Reconnecting — your upload is safe".
  • You do not have to wait. Leave your name, phone number and email in the app and we will email you the link when the scene is live. The build carries on if you close the tab. (Email is set up by whoever runs the server; where it is not, the app says so and the team follows up.)

If something goes wrong#

Every failure is explained with a title, a reason and what to do next — never a raw error. If the message says the problem is on our side, the team is alerted (where the operator has connected alerts) and the same file is worth trying again.

Source: docs/guides/what-you-can-upload.md · rendered in the browser from the repository's Markdown.

Scans#

Room and property captures from a phone or a Matterport camera are a first-class upload. Verse recognises a capture: the exporter names a capture app, the upload is a MatterPak or a PLY mesh, or every material is a single photo texture and nothing else. It then **cleans it before publishing**, in about a second:

Levels the floor and puts it at height 0. It finds the lowest large level surface and rotates it exactly level. Bumps of up to 2.5 cm in it (the "wobbly floor" of a LiDAR mesh) are flattened. Phone captures are usually a fraction of a degree off; up to 45° is corrected.
Removes floating debris. Crumbs and small fragments hanging in the air go. Anything touching the room stays, like a chair on the floor.
Fills small holes. A hole up to 1.2 m round is filled with texture from around it. Windows, doorways and unscanned rooms stay open.
Evens out the light baked into the texture. Dark corners are lifted and hot spots by a window are softened. Colours and the overall brightness are kept: the correction is gentle and never more than ×1.5 / ÷1.5.

The upload screen offers Clean up the scan, on by default; turn it off to publish the capture exactly as exported. Through the API, send X-Verse-Scan: off (or clean to clean a file Verse did not recognise as a capture). The share link's record lists what was done, for example "levelled the floor (it was 0.56° off), removed 119 floating fragments, filled 23 small holes". A scan that fits the product limits (≤ 6 m, ≤ 2 M triangles) opens in Fidelity; a larger one (a corridor, a whole floor, a house) is cleaned and streamed.

What to export, per app#
App	Export	Notes
Polycam	GLB (best), or OBJ (zip it with its .mtl and textures), or USDZ. Point clouds: PLY / XYZ / LAS. Gaussian splats: PLY	Polycam's free plan limits some export formats.
Scaniverse	GLB (best), OBJ (zip) or USDZ. Point clouds: PLY / LAS. Splats: PLY	Scaniverse's SPZ splat format is not read yet; export splats as PLY.
3D Scanner App	GLB (best), OBJ (zip), USDZ, PLY mesh, or PLY / XYZ / LAS points	
iPhone (RoomPlan, Reality Composer, Object Capture)	USDZ	A USDZ that is a capture is cleaned as a scan, not treated as a BIM model.
Matterport	the MatterPak Bundle (.zip), uploaded unchanged	See below. No Matterport login, API key or account link is needed: Verse only reads the file you download.
Photogrammetry (RealityCapture, Metashape, Luma…)	GLB, or OBJ (zip)	
Matterport: which export to ask for#

In Matterport Cloud, open the space and buy or download the **MatterPak™ Bundle** add-on. It is a paid add-on per space, and Matterport decides which spaces offer it. Upload the .zip as it arrives. Verse looks inside:

The textured mesh (<model id>.obj + .mtl + its texture JPGs) is the scene. Matterport writes it Z-up in metres; Verse reads it that way, then cleans it as a scan. A home is usually larger than the Fidelity limits, so it streams.
cloud.xyz (a colourised point cloud) is skipped when the zip is converted as a mesh. To get the point-cloud view instead, upload the same zip with X-Verse-Kind: cloud (or as a separate upload).
The colour plan and ceiling plan images (colorplan_*.jpg, PDF) are listed in the record but not used. Verse draws its own floor plan from the mesh.

Limits of a MatterPak to know about:

Its mesh is Matterport's own simplified reconstruction, with textures of about 2K each. It is not the detail of the 360° panoramas in the Matterport tour, and the panoramas are not in the bundle.
Spaces captured before December 2017 carry only the OBJ.
cloud.xyz is a reduced-density cloud. For survey-grade density, buy the separate E57 add-on and upload the .e57 directly (a point cloud).
A large home's bundle can pass the 512 MB upload limit, usually because of cloud.xyz. Remove it from the zip, or upload the mesh and the cloud separately.
Limits#

These are enforced. A file over a limit is refused before it uploads.

Limit	Value
File size	512 MB; up to 20 GB for a file prepared with verse-prepare (the Blender, Unreal and Unity plug-ins do this) and sent through the resumable upload. The glTF container itself caps one .glb at 4 GB; past that, split the export or instance repeated geometry
Triangles (streamed)	no fixed cap: past 12 M source triangles the build runs region by region in bounded memory (a 1 B-triangle instanced city compiles at a 5 GB peak). The file's 32-bit offsets cap it at 4 GB: about 28 B per unique triangle plus ~2 B per repeated triangle (repeated meshes, 8+ copies, are stored once but each copy keeps its directory entries) — roughly 140 M unique triangles with nothing repeated, or ~50 M unique beside ~1 B repeated
Build time (streamed)	45 minutes in total; each attempt up to 30 minutes (an attempt with no progress for 10 minutes is stopped and retried on lighter settings)
Fidelity file size	512 MB (the upload cap). Over 24 MB the textures stream — a small first view in seconds, then every texture sharpened once to what the device holds; over 1.5 M triangles phones get a simplified mesh, desktops the full one (Fidelity mode)
Single-room interiors in Fidelity	a one-storey room under 100 MB, 2 M triangles and 128 textures streams for phones and opens as itself on desktops from the same link (Fidelity mode)
Splat captures	4,000,000 splats
Uploads	6 per hour anonymously, 20 per hour signed in
Builds at once	2 per server — the rest wait in a queue, and the app shows your place in it
Recommendations (streamed)#

These are recommendations, not limits — larger scenes are attempted, and heal themselves onto lighter settings when they need to.

For a quick, reliable build	Stay around
Triangles	up to about 3 million
Textures	up to about 400
Texture size	2K (2048 px)
File size	up to about 170 MB

The basis is the largest scene we test on every release: 3.1 M triangles, 399 textures, 167 MB — about 20 minutes to build on the production server.

Textures larger than 2048 px are resampled to 2048 px for streaming (the 12 most prominent materials keep 4096 px). A base-colour texture larger than 4096 px (8K, 16K) keeps its full detail: it is cut into pages and the viewer streams only the pages in view (virtual texturing; ?vt=0 shows the old path). Other maps above 2K only make the upload and the build longer. **In Fidelity mode nothing is resampled**: a 4096² map is shown at 4096².

Baked in Blender (bake to emission). If you baked your lighting into images and plugged them into each material's Emission socket — the common archviz workflow, with the Base Color socket often still holding the original albedo texture — the scene is recognised as baked (and streams): every material whose emission image is a lit picture (bright over most of its texels) is shown exactly as that picture, unlit, and its base-colour texture is set aside (it is not downloaded). Cut-out materials keep their holes: the alpha of the base texture still applies to plants and grilles in Alpha Clip or Alpha Blend mode. A material whose emission image is mostly black with a few glowing texels — a screen, a lamp — stays a lit material and is listed in the Lights panel. Naming the baked materials …_Baked (what Blender's bake add-ons do) is a helpful hint, used to pick the right UV map when the bake sits on its own lightmap UVs, but it is not required and does not by itself make a material baked: the pixels decide.

Logos, stickers and posters. A flat image with transparent parts — a company logo on a wall, a sticker, a framed poster with a transparent border, a sign — is a decal: a plane whose base-colour image carries the cut-out in its alpha channel (a PNG on a transparent background). Export it in either Alpha Clip (MASK) or Alpha Blend (BLEND) mode; both work the same way. The image's alpha decides: where it is transparent the wall behind shows through, where it is opaque the picture shows, lit like the surface it sits on, and from both sides if the material is double-sided. Keep the image's transparent pixels truly transparent (alpha 0) — their colour does not matter. What counts as glass instead: an Alpha Blend material whose transparency is partial — a window pane with its alpha factor below 1 and no image, or an image whose alpha is a soft, mid-range tint everywhere (a privacy film) — and any material carrying KHR_materials_transmission. Those refract and transmit; a logo never does.

Compression#
Supported — decoded on our side	Not supported
Draco geometry (KHR_draco_mesh_compression)	AVIF textures
meshopt geometry (EXT_meshopt_compression, KHR_meshopt_compression — gltfpack -c / -cc)	
Quantized meshes (KHR_mesh_quantization)	
WebP textures (EXT_texture_webp)	
KTX2 / Basis textures (KHR_texture_basisu)	
What is rendered#

Every Khronos material renders, on WebGPU and on WebGL2 (iPhones, in-app browsers), in Fidelity mode and in streamed scenes:

The metallic-roughness model: base colour, metalness, roughness, normal, occlusion and emissive maps, vertex colours, alpha mask and blend, and double-sided materials.
KHR_materials_clearcoat, with its clearcoat, roughness and normal textures.
KHR_materials_sheen, with colour and roughness textures.
KHR_materials_specular, with specular and colour textures.
KHR_materials_transmission, with its texture: glass that refracts and takes its base colour.
KHR_materials_volume, with the thickness texture and absorption colour.
KHR_materials_ior, which also changes how much a non-glass surface reflects.
KHR_materials_iridescence: thin film, with the strength and thickness textures.
KHR_materials_anisotropy: brushed metal, with strength, rotation and the direction texture.
KHR_materials_dispersion: rainbow edges in glass.
KHR_materials_emissive_strength, KHR_materials_unlit, and KHR_materials_variants (the default variant).
KHR_texture_transform on every texture: each map can tile, rotate or offset on its own, and a second UV set works too, for example ambient occlusion on TEXCOORD_1. The texture's wrap mode (repeat, clamp, mirror) is honoured.

Fidelity mode also renders punctual lights, node animation, skins and morph targets.

These limits remain:

Phones. The extension textures are smaller on phones (512 px; 256 px for anisotropy and clearcoat-normal maps), at most 24 MB per scene. Past that a material keeps its factors.
Streamed scenes carry the extension textures at up to 512 px, and anisotropy there follows the surface's UV direction (a .vpk has no tangents).
Not in streamed scenes yet: specular-glossiness.

The full table, per backend, is in the Fidelity mode guide. If your file lists such an extension as required, the server relaxes that requirement and builds the scene anyway; the result notes what was skipped.

Animated models#

Node animation (doors, fans, turntables — anything a clip moves as a whole) and skinned meshes (rigged figures) play in the streamed scene, at any file size, on every device; the first clip plays on open and the clip bar switches, pauses and scrubs. In Fidelity mode everything plays, morph targets included. Not carried by the streamed path: morph targets (blend shapes), and skins with more than 256 joints — a model that needs those is published in compatibility mode (the whole model as one download) so it still plays, as long as the file is under about 96 MB.

Who can open the link#

Anyone with a current browser. Browsers with WebGPU — Chrome, Edge, Safari 26, Firefox on Windows and macOS — get the full picture. Others (older iPhones and iPads, many in-app browsers) get a WebGL2 build that streams the same scene, with walk, tour, review pins and video export, and the same studio lighting, sun and contact shadows, bloom, optional ambient occlusion, per-room reflection probes, real-time GI and uploaded HDR backgrounds. Still WebGPU-only: path-traced stills, screen-space and ray-traced reflections, temporal upscaling, HDR display output and Gaussian-splat captures. The full table is in Browser support.

What the preflight checks#

Before uploading, the app reads only the head of your file and reports:

Red — blocks the upload: over the size limit; not a format we read; a model that references files that were not uploaded; no meshes; lines or points instead of triangles; a compression we cannot decode; a damaged or truncated file.
Amber — you can continue: more triangles or textures than we recommend; textures larger than 2K; a build likely to be long; a material feature that will be skipped; animations on a model too large for compatibility mode (it is built static).
Green: what it found — meshes, triangles, textures, animations that will play — and how long the build should take.
What is this? the classification (product / scan / interior / building / BIM / point cloud), its evidence, and the road it will take — correctable with one tap.
How should it look? a studio preset and background for a product; the Lighting choice for a scene.

The server runs the same checks — and the same classifier — again on the bytes that arrive, so API and exporter uploads get the same answers (see the API reference).

While it builds#
Time left is a real countdown ("About 6 min left"). It never counts up; if a build overruns its estimate the app says so. A Fidelity upload is live in seconds and the app says so.
If a build struggles, it heals itself. A build that runs out of memory or time is retried automatically — up to three attempts — with lighter texture settings. You will see a note such as "rebuilding with lighter texture settings — no action needed". Nothing else about the scene changes.
You always get a working link. Every finished scene is checked before it goes live. If a build cannot be made to work even with the lightest settings, we publish your model in compatibility mode instead: the same model at full quality as one larger download (for models up to about 96 MB). The app tells you when that happened.
A dropped connection is not an error. Uploads resume by themselves from where they stopped — through Wi-Fi drops and server restarts. You will see "Reconnecting — your upload is safe".
You do not have to wait. Leave your name, phone number and email in the app and we will email you the link when the scene is live. The build carries on if you close the tab. (Email is set up by whoever runs the server; where it is not, the app says so and the team follows up.)
If something goes wrong#

Every failure is explained with a title, a reason and what to do next — never a raw error. If the message says the problem is on our side, the team is alerted (where the operator has connected alerts) and the same file is worth trying again.
