How-to guides

Fidelity mode#

A single product renders exactly as exported. A city streams. Fidelity mode (2.8) is the first half of that sentence: for an upload that is one object or a small set — a shoe, a chair, a lamp, a hovercar, a scan — the server publishes the file itself and the viewer shows it the way a plain glTF viewer would, with the textures and materials you exported, under studio lighting, in seconds. Nothing in between can lose a texture.

What happens when you upload#

  1. We look at the file before a byte is sent. The upload screen reads the head of the file in your browser — meshes, triangles, textures and their sizes, materials, lights, baked or live lighting, the model's bounds — and the same classifier runs again on the server with the bytes that arrive (web/playground/asset-class.js, one module, two places, one verdict).
  2. Step 1 — What is this? The app says what it found in plain words ("We found: a product — 1 mesh, 3 textures (2,048²), 404,476 triangles, PBR materials. We'll show it in Fidelity mode…"), shows the evidence as chips, and lets you correct it with one tap: **Product / Scan / Interior / Building / BIM / Point cloud** — only the plausible ones are enabled — plus Show as: Fidelity | Streamed.
  3. Step 2 — How should it look? A product or scan picks a studio environment (Neutral, Warm, Dark) and a background (studio, pure white, or a colour). A scene keeps the existing Lighting choice (keep as exported / bake preview / bake final).
  4. Publish. One button. Nothing advances or starts by itself.
  5. When it is live, the app says what we detected and did ("Shown in Fidelity mode: exact textures and materials, studio lighting, no streaming"), and the share link opens it: /view?glb=ingest/<id>.fidelity.glb (/app?glb=… for the workspace). Studio shows a Fidelity badge on the scene.

A textured product is live in about a second (the shoe: 1.8 s from the click to the link, 0.8 s on the server).

The rules#

VerdictRulePath
productone object or a small set: longest side ≤ 6 m, ≤ 10 M triangles after Draco decode, ≤ 48 textures, ≤ 4 GB decoded (fifteen 8K maps), no IFC/USD, no room signature (≥ 40 meshes with ≥ 24 materials and lights or a > 3.5 m extent), not lightmap-bakedFidelity — unless it has no textures and under 50 k triangles: nothing to keep exact, so it streams (seconds) and the app offers Fidelity as the alternative
scanone to four dense meshes (≥ 300 k triangles) with one to three textures of ≥ 4096² — or ≥ 800 k triangles in ≤ 2 materialsFidelity while it fits the product caps; a bigger scan is a scene
interior / buildingeverything else: large bounds, many materials, lightmap bakes, a room's worth of meshes and lights (> 25 m across = building)Streamed (the .vpk compiler, level-of-detail geometry and texture streaming)
bim / cloud / splatIFC, USD, point clouds, Gaussian splatsalways streamed

A Fidelity request past the hard caps (over the 512 MB ceiling, more than 20 M triangles or 8 GB of decoded textures) streams instead, and the app says why ("Streamed instead of Fidelity mode: …").

What the server publishes#

  • ingest/<id>.fidelity.glb — the upload with its Draco geometry decoded and every texture at its source resolution and format: a PNG stays a PNG, a 4096² map stays 4096². No verse-prepare right-sizing, no re-encode, no .vpk compile.
  • ingest/<id>.fidelity.tex.json + ingest/<id>.fidelity.tex (files over 24 MB) — the texture pyramid the viewer streams from; and ingest/<id>.fidelity.phone.glb past 1.5 M triangles — the phone mesh. Sidecars: a plain glTF viewer opens the .fidelity.glb without them.
  • ingest/<id>.usdz — the AR Quick Look package, from the same bytes.
  • ingest/<id>.poster.png — the poster the viewer attaches on first open.
  • The job record (GET /v1/ingest/<job>): path: "fidelity", glbUrl, classification (the verdict and its evidence), look (the studio preset and background you chose), digest (sha256:…) and signature (the digest under the server's signing key), stats { mode: "fidelity", tris, meshes, textures, bytes }.
  • Private, unlisted, share tokens, versions and delete work exactly as for a .vpk: the artifact is a scene file like any other.

The API takes the same road with X-Verse-Path: fidelity (or path in the resumable begin body); an upload that says nothing streams as it always has, and the record still carries the verdict so your tool can decide. The JS SDK: verse.upload(file, { path: "fidelity", look: "studio:warm,bg:ffffff" }).

What the viewer renders#

Fidelity mode is the engine's classic (whole-file) path hardened into a reference-grade glTF viewer — on WebGPU and on the WebGL2 build:

  • Metallic-roughness PBR with the Khronos BRDF: GGX / height-correlated Smith / Schlick, multiple-scattering energy compensation, exact sRGB ↔ linear handling, textures uploaded at source resolution with a full mip chain (box-filtered in linear light) and 16× anisotropic filtering.
  • Image-based lighting from a prefiltered environment: GGX specular mips (a 256² cube in Fidelity mode) plus SH9 irradiance; three studio presets (neutral, warm, dark-contrast), generated on the device, deterministic. The WebGL2 build lights with its analytic rig (the same gradient, the preset as a tint) — no prefiltered cube on that tier yet.
  • Every extension the loader reads, rendered or not (be honest):
    ExtensionRendered
    KHR_materials_emissive_strength, KHR_materials_unlit, KHR_texture_basisu, EXT_texture_webp, KHR_draco_mesh_compression, KHR_mesh_quantizationyes
    KHR_texture_transformyes — per texture, plus one second UV set and the sampler's wrap mode
    KHR_materials_clearcoat, KHR_materials_sheenyes — factors and every texture (clearcoat normal included)
    KHR_materials_transmission, KHR_materials_ior, KHR_materials_volumeyes — screen-space refraction tinted by the base colour, the transmission and thickness textures, per-pixel absorption in world units; an authored IOR sets every dielectric's reflectance
    KHR_materials_specularyes — factors and textures
    KHR_materials_dispersionyes — one refraction per colour channel
    KHR_materials_variantsthe default variant; setVariant switches (classic scenes)
    KHR_lights_punctualyes (listed in the Lights panel)
    KHR_materials_iridescenceyes — thin-film interference, strength and thickness textures
    KHR_materials_anisotropyyes — anisotropic GGX + bent-normal environment, strength / rotation / direction texture
    vertex colours, alpha MASK / BLEND, double-sided, morph targets, skins, node animationyes (BLEND through weighted-blended order-independent transparency — not depth-sorted)
  • Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapping by default (?tone=aces for the filmic curve), 4× MSAA (or TSR with ?temporal), a soft **contact shadow** under the model (?contact=0..1, default 0.6, WebGPU), auto framing from the model's bounds, orbit controls with a slow turntable until the first interaction (?turntable=0 holds the authored yaw; walking is still there for anything over 4 m).
  • Share links keep the look: /view?glb=…&look=studio:warm,bg:ffffff; ?env=neutral|warm|dark and ?bg= on the link still win.

Measured#

web/test/fidelity-gltf.mjs renders the Khronos glTF-Sample-Assets set (DamagedHelmet, FlightHelmet, SciFiHelmet, BoomBox, WaterBottle, Corset, Lantern, ToyCar, MaterialsVariantsShoe, ClearCoatTest, TransmissionTest, IridescenceLamp) plus a real customer shoe model in Fidelity mode and with a pinned reference renderer at the same camera, the same environment (the engine's neutral studio radiance handed to the reference as a float equirect), the same tone curve and backdrop, then compares ΔE2000 over the model's pixels. The gate: mean ΔE ≤ 6 on the core-PBR set and ≤ 10 on the extension set (WebGL2: +3), a texture-detail ratio ≥ 0.5 (no clay), mean luminance ≥ 0.03 (no black), no console errors, both backends; then the upload path end to end.

Larger products#

A furniture catalogue piece with a 4K–8K texture set, a car, a watch with a 5 M-triangle mesh: previously anything over 96 MB could not be held whole in a browser, so it streamed through the .vpk compiler and lost the exact look. Now a Fidelity product of any size up to the 512 MB upload cap loads progressively, and the full-quality frame is the one the 2.8 viewer rendered.

On publish. Past 24 MB (VERSE_FIDELITY_STREAM_MB) the server runs verse-prepare --fidelity-pyramid on the published GLB and writes, beside it, a texture pyramid: every texture at half, quarter, … of its source down to 128 px (<id>.fidelity.tex, each level a complete JPEG or PNG — JPEG q92 for colour maps without alpha, PNG for data maps and anything ≤ 256 px) and a manifest (<id>.fidelity.tex.json: where the GLB's JSON chunk, each image's bytes and every geometry buffer view sit, which images are colour / extension-packed / alpha, and the levels). The levels are written tier by tier from the smallest, so "every texture at its smallest level" is one byte range. A PNG level is the pixels the viewer's own capped decode would produce (the same image crate call), so the slots the renderer caps anyway — the extension textures at 2048² on desktop — are bit-identical. Past 1.5 M triangles (VERSE_FIDELITY_PHONE_TRIS) the server also writes <id>.fidelity.phone.glb: the same materials and image indices, textures stripped to one 1×1 placeholder, the mesh meshopt-simplified (borders locked, normals and UVs steering the collapse) under an error that starts at 0.05 % of the model's size and doubles until the mesh is under the cap. Desktops never see it. The pyramid for a 15 × 8K set takes about 7 s; the job settles after it, so the first viewer already streams. A product under 24 MB publishes exactly as before — no sidecars, the same bytes, the same load.

In the viewer. ?glb=ingest/<id>.fidelity.glb hands the URL to the render worker, which asks for the manifest. Without one (a small product, an older publish) it fetches the file whole, as 2.8 did. With one:

  1. First view — the GLB's JSON chunk, every non-image buffer view (the geometry; on a phone with a phone mesh, that file's geometry instead) and the smallest level of every texture, by Range requests coalesced across small gaps, four in flight; repacked here into one small GLB the engine loads exactly as any other (same loader, same materials, same image indices). Images a material extension packs load at the renderer's cap (2048 desktop / 512 phone) in this phase, so those slots match today's capped decode from the start.
  2. Refine — each texture once, colour maps first, to one final tier for the whole set: the source bytes out of the GLB on desktop class when they fit the renderer's memory budget (1.5 GB on tier A), else the largest pyramid tier that does; on phone class (tier B, tier C phones, in-app browsers) the largest tier under the 256 MB budget with 32 MB kept free, never past 2048². refine_texture decodes the bytes exactly as a load decodes a Fidelity texture (source resolution, Lanczos3 cap at
    1. and re-uploads with the same mip chain; WebGPU rebuilds the materials' bind groups, WebGL2 refills the shared texture object. One load per texture, no eviction, no level swaps, and nothing is fetched after the last texture lands — orbiting a finished product makes zero requests. A GPU recovery (the engine reloads the first-view GLB from its cache) refines again, once.

The worker posts fidelity-stream messages (first-view, refine ×n, complete: bytes, firstViewMs, fullMs, the tier and the level each image ended at), the status line counts the sharpening, the result says "first view … · sharpening to source resolution", and the HUD's stats carry fidelity. ?fidstream=0 forces the whole-file load (the reference the gate compares against).

GPU-compressed textures. Every image in the pyramid also carries a UASTC mip chain (.basis, capped at 4096², the streamed path's encoder). The decode pool transcodes it to what the device has — BC7 on desktops, ASTC or ETC2 elsewhere — and the renderer uploads the chain as is, one byte per texel plus mips: a quarter of RGBA8. A product takes its source bytes when they fit the budget (the whole-file frame, ΔE 0) and the compressed chains when they do not (helmet-8k: 15 × 8K shown at 4096² compressed instead of RGBA8 4096²); a room always takes them.

Single-room interiors. A room-sized interior — one storey (≤ 6 m high), ≤ 20 m across, ≤ 2 M triangles, ≤ 128 textures, ≤ 2 GB decoded, under 100 MB — is flagged roomFidelity by the classifier. It streams as always (that is what phones load: the one-time fit-mode load), and the server publishes it as itself beside the .vpk (<id>.fidelity.glb + the pyramid, seconds, before the minutes-long compile). From the same ?vpk= link a desktop-class device (tier A, tier C desktop) opens the room in Fidelity: the render worker finds the manifest beside the .vpk and loads the room progressively — geometry and every texture at ≤ 128 px first, then each texture's compressed chain at the largest size the set holds under 320 MB of texture memory — with the exact materials, no atlas, no cluster cut, sharp from the first view; staging (stage.json spawn, walk mode) and the floor plan work as before because the scene id is the .vpk's. A phone streams the same room in the same tone curve the desktop's Fidelity road shows (Khronos PBR Neutral), so the link looks the same on both. ?roomfid=0 keeps the streamed road and today's curve on any device (the comparison baseline). A customer reception (48 MB, 96 textures, 14.8 m) is the gate's case, compared with a reference viewer page.

Honest limits. Textures are RGBA8 on the exact path, so what fits uncompressed is what a GPU holds: five 8K maps are 1.3 GB at level 0. Compressed chains are capped at 4096² and are lossy (UASTC, pack level 1 — the streamed path's quality); a product that fits as RGBA8 never takes them. Phones never take the compressed chains on this path yet (they hold RGBA8 at ≤ 2048²; rooms stream on phones). Geometry is not streamed: a desktop fetches the full mesh before the first view (a 6 M-triangle product is 211 MB of geometry — about 90 s on a 20 Mbit/s line), and a phone the phone mesh. A product whose full set fits the budget (the chess set, a 4K helmet) renders the 2.8 frame at full quality — measured ΔE2000 against the whole-file load in web/test/fix-verify-bigfidelity.mjs.

Background#

What sits behind the model is an owner setting, a link knob and an embed verb — one spec string everywhere:

SpecMeaning
rrggbba solid colour, exact (the engine's sky pass paints it)
transparentnothing — the host page shows through (embeds)
grad:rrggbb,rrggbba vertical gradient, top → bottom
studio:neutral · studio:warm · studio:darkone of the studio environments as the backdrop; it lights the model too
image:ingest/<id>.bg.jpgan uploaded picture (.jpg/.png ≤ 20 MB), cover-fit, backdrop only
hdr:ingest/<id>.bg.hdran uploaded Radiance .hdr (≤ 20 MB): the backdrop and the image-based lighting
  • Owners: the Background chip in the stage chrome (signed in) — six presets including pure white and the indigo-slate default, a colour picker, a two-colour gradient, the three studio environments, and a picture/HDR upload. Saved as the scene's <id>.bg.json sidecar (PUT /v1/scenes/<id>/background, PUT …/background/image) under the scene's own visibility and delete rules, and replayed for every visitor on both backends.
  • Links: ?bg= on any share link wins over the saved one.
  • Embeds: bg in the options ("transparent" when your page wants its own), viewer.setBackground(spec), viewer.getBackground(), the background event.
  • Honest limits: a gradient, a picture and transparent are drawn by the page behind a canvas created with an alpha surface, so switching to one of them on a page that opened opaque reloads the page once; .exr is not read yet (upload an .hdr); the WebGL2 build ignores an uploaded HDR (its lighting stays the analytic studio rig).

HOW-TO GUIDES
Fidelity mode#

A single product renders exactly as exported. A city streams. Fidelity mode (2.8) is the first half of that sentence: for an upload that is one object or a small set — a shoe, a chair, a lamp, a hovercar, a scan — the server publishes the file itself and the viewer shows it the way a plain glTF viewer would, with the textures and materials you exported, under studio lighting, in seconds. Nothing in between can lose a texture.

What happens when you upload#
We look at the file before a byte is sent. The upload screen reads the head of the file in your browser — meshes, triangles, textures and their sizes, materials, lights, baked or live lighting, the model's bounds — and the same classifier runs again on the server with the bytes that arrive (web/playground/asset-class.js, one module, two places, one verdict).
Step 1 — What is this? The app says what it found in plain words ("We found: a product — 1 mesh, 3 textures (2,048²), 404,476 triangles, PBR materials. We'll show it in Fidelity mode…"), shows the evidence as chips, and lets you correct it with one tap: **Product / Scan / Interior / Building / BIM / Point cloud** — only the plausible ones are enabled — plus Show as: Fidelity | Streamed.
Step 2 — How should it look? A product or scan picks a studio environment (Neutral, Warm, Dark) and a background (studio, pure white, or a colour). A scene keeps the existing Lighting choice (keep as exported / bake preview / bake final).
Publish. One button. Nothing advances or starts by itself.
When it is live, the app says what we detected and did ("Shown in Fidelity mode: exact textures and materials, studio lighting, no streaming"), and the share link opens it: /view?glb=ingest/<id>.fidelity.glb (/app?glb=… for the workspace). Studio shows a Fidelity badge on the scene.

A textured product is live in about a second (the shoe: 1.8 s from the click to the link, 0.8 s on the server).

The rules#
Verdict	Rule	Path
product	one object or a small set: longest side ≤ 6 m, ≤ 10 M triangles after Draco decode, ≤ 48 textures, ≤ 4 GB decoded (fifteen 8K maps), no IFC/USD, no room signature (≥ 40 meshes with ≥ 24 materials and lights or a > 3.5 m extent), not lightmap-baked	Fidelity — unless it has no textures and under 50 k triangles: nothing to keep exact, so it streams (seconds) and the app offers Fidelity as the alternative
scan	one to four dense meshes (≥ 300 k triangles) with one to three textures of ≥ 4096² — or ≥ 800 k triangles in ≤ 2 materials	Fidelity while it fits the product caps; a bigger scan is a scene
interior / building	everything else: large bounds, many materials, lightmap bakes, a room's worth of meshes and lights (> 25 m across = building)	Streamed (the .vpk compiler, level-of-detail geometry and texture streaming)
bim / cloud / splat	IFC, USD, point clouds, Gaussian splats	always streamed

A Fidelity request past the hard caps (over the 512 MB ceiling, more than 20 M triangles or 8 GB of decoded textures) streams instead, and the app says why ("Streamed instead of Fidelity mode: …").

What the server publishes#
ingest/<id>.fidelity.glb — the upload with its Draco geometry decoded and every texture at its source resolution and format: a PNG stays a PNG, a 4096² map stays 4096². No verse-prepare right-sizing, no re-encode, no .vpk compile.
ingest/<id>.fidelity.tex.json + ingest/<id>.fidelity.tex (files over 24 MB) — the texture pyramid the viewer streams from; and ingest/<id>.fidelity.phone.glb past 1.5 M triangles — the phone mesh. Sidecars: a plain glTF viewer opens the .fidelity.glb without them.
ingest/<id>.usdz — the AR Quick Look package, from the same bytes.
ingest/<id>.poster.png — the poster the viewer attaches on first open.
The job record (GET /v1/ingest/<job>): path: "fidelity", glbUrl, classification (the verdict and its evidence), look (the studio preset and background you chose), digest (sha256:…) and signature (the digest under the server's signing key), stats { mode: "fidelity", tris, meshes, textures, bytes }.
Private, unlisted, share tokens, versions and delete work exactly as for a .vpk: the artifact is a scene file like any other.

The API takes the same road with X-Verse-Path: fidelity (or path in the resumable begin body); an upload that says nothing streams as it always has, and the record still carries the verdict so your tool can decide. The JS SDK: verse.upload(file, { path: "fidelity", look: "studio:warm,bg:ffffff" }).

What the viewer renders#

Fidelity mode is the engine's classic (whole-file) path hardened into a reference-grade glTF viewer — on WebGPU and on the WebGL2 build:

Metallic-roughness PBR with the Khronos BRDF: GGX / height-correlated Smith / Schlick, multiple-scattering energy compensation, exact sRGB ↔ linear handling, textures uploaded at source resolution with a full mip chain (box-filtered in linear light) and 16× anisotropic filtering.
Image-based lighting from a prefiltered environment: GGX specular mips (a 256² cube in Fidelity mode) plus SH9 irradiance; three studio presets (neutral, warm, dark-contrast), generated on the device, deterministic. The WebGL2 build lights with its analytic rig (the same gradient, the preset as a tint) — no prefiltered cube on that tier yet.
Every extension the loader reads, rendered or not (be honest):
Extension	Rendered
KHR_materials_emissive_strength, KHR_materials_unlit, KHR_texture_basisu, EXT_texture_webp, KHR_draco_mesh_compression, KHR_mesh_quantization	yes
KHR_texture_transform	yes — per texture, plus one second UV set and the sampler's wrap mode
KHR_materials_clearcoat, KHR_materials_sheen	yes — factors and every texture (clearcoat normal included)
KHR_materials_transmission, KHR_materials_ior, KHR_materials_volume	yes — screen-space refraction tinted by the base colour, the transmission and thickness textures, per-pixel absorption in world units; an authored IOR sets every dielectric's reflectance
KHR_materials_specular	yes — factors and textures
KHR_materials_dispersion	yes — one refraction per colour channel
KHR_materials_variants	the default variant; setVariant switches (classic scenes)
KHR_lights_punctual	yes (listed in the Lights panel)
KHR_materials_iridescence	yes — thin-film interference, strength and thickness textures
KHR_materials_anisotropy	yes — anisotropic GGX + bent-normal environment, strength / rotation / direction texture
vertex colours, alpha MASK / BLEND, double-sided, morph targets, skins, node animation	yes (BLEND through weighted-blended order-independent transparency — not depth-sorted)
Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapping by default (?tone=aces for the filmic curve), 4× MSAA (or TSR with ?temporal), a soft **contact shadow** under the model (?contact=0..1, default 0.6, WebGPU), auto framing from the model's bounds, orbit controls with a slow turntable until the first interaction (?turntable=0 holds the authored yaw; walking is still there for anything over 4 m).
Share links keep the look: /view?glb=…&look=studio:warm,bg:ffffff; ?env=neutral|warm|dark and ?bg= on the link still win.
Measured#

web/test/fidelity-gltf.mjs renders the Khronos glTF-Sample-Assets set (DamagedHelmet, FlightHelmet, SciFiHelmet, BoomBox, WaterBottle, Corset, Lantern, ToyCar, MaterialsVariantsShoe, ClearCoatTest, TransmissionTest, IridescenceLamp) plus a real customer shoe model in Fidelity mode and with a pinned reference renderer at the same camera, the same environment (the engine's neutral studio radiance handed to the reference as a float equirect), the same tone curve and backdrop, then compares ΔE2000 over the model's pixels. The gate: mean ΔE ≤ 6 on the core-PBR set and ≤ 10 on the extension set (WebGL2: +3), a texture-detail ratio ≥ 0.5 (no clay), mean luminance ≥ 0.03 (no black), no console errors, both backends; then the upload path end to end.

Larger products#

A furniture catalogue piece with a 4K–8K texture set, a car, a watch with a 5 M-triangle mesh: previously anything over 96 MB could not be held whole in a browser, so it streamed through the .vpk compiler and lost the exact look. Now a Fidelity product of any size up to the 512 MB upload cap loads progressively, and the full-quality frame is the one the 2.8 viewer rendered.

On publish. Past 24 MB (VERSE_FIDELITY_STREAM_MB) the server runs verse-prepare --fidelity-pyramid on the published GLB and writes, beside it, a texture pyramid: every texture at half, quarter, … of its source down to 128 px (<id>.fidelity.tex, each level a complete JPEG or PNG — JPEG q92 for colour maps without alpha, PNG for data maps and anything ≤ 256 px) and a manifest (<id>.fidelity.tex.json: where the GLB's JSON chunk, each image's bytes and every geometry buffer view sit, which images are colour / extension-packed / alpha, and the levels). The levels are written tier by tier from the smallest, so "every texture at its smallest level" is one byte range. A PNG level is the pixels the viewer's own capped decode would produce (the same image crate call), so the slots the renderer caps anyway — the extension textures at 2048² on desktop — are bit-identical. Past 1.5 M triangles (VERSE_FIDELITY_PHONE_TRIS) the server also writes <id>.fidelity.phone.glb: the same materials and image indices, textures stripped to one 1×1 placeholder, the mesh meshopt-simplified (borders locked, normals and UVs steering the collapse) under an error that starts at 0.05 % of the model's size and doubles until the mesh is under the cap. Desktops never see it. The pyramid for a 15 × 8K set takes about 7 s; the job settles after it, so the first viewer already streams. A product under 24 MB publishes exactly as before — no sidecars, the same bytes, the same load.

In the viewer. ?glb=ingest/<id>.fidelity.glb hands the URL to the render worker, which asks for the manifest. Without one (a small product, an older publish) it fetches the file whole, as 2.8 did. With one:

First view — the GLB's JSON chunk, every non-image buffer view (the geometry; on a phone with a phone mesh, that file's geometry instead) and the smallest level of every texture, by Range requests coalesced across small gaps, four in flight; repacked here into one small GLB the engine loads exactly as any other (same loader, same materials, same image indices). Images a material extension packs load at the renderer's cap (2048 desktop / 512 phone) in this phase, so those slots match today's capped decode from the start.
Refine — each texture once, colour maps first, to one final tier for the whole set: the source bytes out of the GLB on desktop class when they fit the renderer's memory budget (1.5 GB on tier A), else the largest pyramid tier that does; on phone class (tier B, tier C phones, in-app browsers) the largest tier under the 256 MB budget with 32 MB kept free, never past 2048². refine_texture decodes the bytes exactly as a load decodes a Fidelity texture (source resolution, Lanczos3 cap at
and re-uploads with the same mip chain; WebGPU rebuilds the materials' bind groups, WebGL2 refills the shared texture object. One load per texture, no eviction, no level swaps, and nothing is fetched after the last texture lands — orbiting a finished product makes zero requests. A GPU recovery (the engine reloads the first-view GLB from its cache) refines again, once.

The worker posts fidelity-stream messages (first-view, refine ×n, complete: bytes, firstViewMs, fullMs, the tier and the level each image ended at), the status line counts the sharpening, the result says "first view … · sharpening to source resolution", and the HUD's stats carry fidelity. ?fidstream=0 forces the whole-file load (the reference the gate compares against).

GPU-compressed textures. Every image in the pyramid also carries a UASTC mip chain (.basis, capped at 4096², the streamed path's encoder). The decode pool transcodes it to what the device has — BC7 on desktops, ASTC or ETC2 elsewhere — and the renderer uploads the chain as is, one byte per texel plus mips: a quarter of RGBA8. A product takes its source bytes when they fit the budget (the whole-file frame, ΔE 0) and the compressed chains when they do not (helmet-8k: 15 × 8K shown at 4096² compressed instead of RGBA8 4096²); a room always takes them.

Single-room interiors. A room-sized interior — one storey (≤ 6 m high), ≤ 20 m across, ≤ 2 M triangles, ≤ 128 textures, ≤ 2 GB decoded, under 100 MB — is flagged roomFidelity by the classifier. It streams as always (that is what phones load: the one-time fit-mode load), and the server publishes it as itself beside the .vpk (<id>.fidelity.glb + the pyramid, seconds, before the minutes-long compile). From the same ?vpk= link a desktop-class device (tier A, tier C desktop) opens the room in Fidelity: the render worker finds the manifest beside the .vpk and loads the room progressively — geometry and every texture at ≤ 128 px first, then each texture's compressed chain at the largest size the set holds under 320 MB of texture memory — with the exact materials, no atlas, no cluster cut, sharp from the first view; staging (stage.json spawn, walk mode) and the floor plan work as before because the scene id is the .vpk's. A phone streams the same room in the same tone curve the desktop's Fidelity road shows (Khronos PBR Neutral), so the link looks the same on both. ?roomfid=0 keeps the streamed road and today's curve on any device (the comparison baseline). A customer reception (48 MB, 96 textures, 14.8 m) is the gate's case, compared with a reference viewer page.

Honest limits. Textures are RGBA8 on the exact path, so what fits uncompressed is what a GPU holds: five 8K maps are 1.3 GB at level 0. Compressed chains are capped at 4096² and are lossy (UASTC, pack level 1 — the streamed path's quality); a product that fits as RGBA8 never takes them. Phones never take the compressed chains on this path yet (they hold RGBA8 at ≤ 2048²; rooms stream on phones). Geometry is not streamed: a desktop fetches the full mesh before the first view (a 6 M-triangle product is 211 MB of geometry — about 90 s on a 20 Mbit/s line), and a phone the phone mesh. A product whose full set fits the budget (the chess set, a 4K helmet) renders the 2.8 frame at full quality — measured ΔE2000 against the whole-file load in web/test/fix-verify-bigfidelity.mjs.

Background#

What sits behind the model is an owner setting, a link knob and an embed verb — one spec string everywhere:

Spec	Meaning
rrggbb	a solid colour, exact (the engine's sky pass paints it)
transparent	nothing — the host page shows through (embeds)
grad:rrggbb,rrggbb	a vertical gradient, top → bottom
studio:neutral · studio:warm · studio:dark	one of the studio environments as the backdrop; it lights the model too
image:ingest/<id>.bg.jpg	an uploaded picture (.jpg/.png ≤ 20 MB), cover-fit, backdrop only
hdr:ingest/<id>.bg.hdr	an uploaded Radiance .hdr (≤ 20 MB): the backdrop and the image-based lighting
Owners: the Background chip in the stage chrome (signed in) — six presets including pure white and the indigo-slate default, a colour picker, a two-colour gradient, the three studio environments, and a picture/HDR upload. Saved as the scene's <id>.bg.json sidecar (PUT /v1/scenes/<id>/background, PUT …/background/image) under the scene's own visibility and delete rules, and replayed for every visitor on both backends.
Links: ?bg= on any share link wins over the saved one.
Embeds: bg in the options ("transparent" when your page wants its own), viewer.setBackground(spec), viewer.getBackground(), the background event.
Honest limits: a gradient, a picture and transparent are drawn by the page behind a canvas created with an alpha surface, so switching to one of them on a page that opened opaque reloads the page once; .exr is not read yet (upload an .hdr); the WebGL2 build ignores an uploaded HDR (its lighting stays the analytic studio rig).

/guides/tour-together.html:
How-to guides

Tour together, live#

Walk a buyer through a home from wherever they are. You open the scene, tap Tour together, and send one link. Whoever opens it — on any phone, from WhatsApp or Instagram's in-app browser, with no account and nothing to install — lands in the same scene and follows your camera. They can break away to look around, rejoin, see where everyone else is, and point at things; you can open hotspots and change styles for the whole group as you talk.

You need: a published scene (an ingest/… link — a scene you uploaded, so the link opens for someone with no file of their own). No account is needed by you or your guests. Everyone can talk with **Join voice** (see Voice below).

1. Start the tour#

Open the scene in /app or on its /view link and tap Tour together (in the share row; on a phone or a /view page it is the Tour together chip in the scene tools). A card appears with:

  • a QR code a guest can scan from a laptop screen,
  • the short link (https://…/t/<code>) with Copy,
  • Share invite — the phone's own share sheet (WhatsApp, Messages, Mail…) where the browser has one, or Start touring on a desktop,
  • WhatsApp, which opens the message ready to send.

From that moment you are the host: the room has your camera as its reference, your minimap is on, and the viewers panel (bottom right) shows everyone who joins.

Invite (in the tour panel) sends the link again at any time. On a phone it opens the share sheet straight away: pick the chat, send, come back — you are still hosting, in the same place, and everyone is still following you. On a desktop it copies the link ("Invite link copied — paste it into WhatsApp") and shows the card with the QR code.

A link lasts a day and opens the same room each time; up to 32 people share a room. The code only shortens the room name — the room name is the secret, so share the link only with the people you want in the tour.

The tour chip#

On a phone the panel folds into one chip at the bottom right, so the home keeps the screen. It always says where things stand:

The chip saysMeaning
Waiting for viewers…You are hosting; nobody has joined yet.
Presenting · 3 in tourYou are hosting; everyone follows your camera.
Following Vinay · 3You are a guest, following the host.
Vinay stepped awayThe host's phone is in another app; look around meanwhile.
· 1 awaySomeone's phone is in another app; they are still in the tour.
Reconnecting…The network dropped; it heals on its own.

Tap the chip to open the full panel (everyone in the tour, Invite, Point, End tour). The round mic button beside it is voice — see Voice below.

2. What a guest sees#

The link opens the scene in the immersive layout. On a phone the usual Enter experience gate comes first (the tap is what lets the browser go full screen), then a small chip asks for a name — optional, kept only in that browser tab (so a reload does not ask again), never stored on the server. Then:

  • their camera follows yours — smoothly, a second behind, with a "Following <your name>" chip and a Take control button;
  • the viewers panel lists everyone, with you marked (host);
  • every other guest is a coloured avatar in the scene and a dot on the minimap, in the colour of their row in the panel.

Break away / rejoin. Take control gives a guest their own camera (the veil goes away; your hotspot and style actions no longer apply to them). Rejoin the tour in the tour bar (or the chip at the top) puts them back behind your camera.

Look here. Anyone — host or guest — taps Point in the tour bar and then something in the scene: a pulsing ring appears at that spot on every screen, with the pointer's name, for a few seconds. On a phone Point stays on until tapped again; on a desktop one click sends one ping.

Hotspots and styles. While hosting, every hotspot you open, variant or style you pick, light change, section cut and guided-tour step is applied on the guests' screens as you make it (the same channel as Present a scene).

3. Switching apps, losing signal, reloading#

Phones leave the browser all the time — to send the invite on WhatsApp, to take a call. The tour is built for it:

  • When you (the host) switch apps, every guest sees a calm card — "Vinay stepped away — the tour continues when they're back" — and gets their own camera to look around meanwhile. Nothing freezes without a word. When you come back, the card goes and everyone glides back behind your camera on their own; you are still hosting, in the same spot, and a small "Back in the tour" chip says so.
  • When a guest switches apps, your panel marks them away (and the chip says "· 1 away"). When they come back they are following you again — no tap needed.
  • If the phone closed the page in the background (iPhones do this to save memory), coming back reloads it straight into the same tour: same role, same name, same place in the home, voice back on if it was on. The others only ever saw "stepped away".
  • Wi-Fi to 4G, a tunnel, a weak signal: the tour reconnects on its own in the background. Only if the network stays down for a while does the chip say Reconnecting….

If the viewer has to restart its graphics (a phone running out of memory), the page goes straight back into the same tour in the same role.

If you close the page for good, guests see "The agent left the tour" within a few seconds and keep their own cameras; the room stays open, so coming back on the same link puts you back in charge. Any guest can also take over with Host this tour in the tour bar.

Faster for late joiners. Once a tour starts, each phone quietly saves the rest of the home to its own storage in the background, so walking into a new room — or coming back after a break — does not wait on the network. It is skipped when the phone is in data-saver mode or on a slow connection, and it never takes more than a modest share of the phone's storage.

4. Hand over and end#

  • Hand over on a guest's row makes them the host; everyone follows them.
  • End tour gives everyone their own camera and shows "The tour has ended". Host again restarts it in the same room.

5. What is recorded#

Nothing from the tour is kept: poses live in memory for 10 s (10 minutes for someone who stepped away), names ride the roster only, the invite table holds {scene, room, expiry} and nothing else, and no audio or video exists. The one trace is analytics: a session that was part of a live tour counts as a live tour in the scene's analytics (Studio → Analytics shows Live tours beside views and enquiries; the CSV carries live_tour_sessions). The same privacy rules as the rest of analytics apply — no names, no addresses.

Voice#

Everyone in the tour can talk. Tap the round mic button on the tour chip (or Join voice in the panel); the browser asks for the microphone once. Then the mic shows its state at a glance:

  • green — your mic is on; it glows while you speak. Tap to mute.
  • red, crossed out — muted. Tap to unmute, or press and hold to talk just while you hold it (like a walkie-talkie), then let go.

Up to six people speak at a time; voices are spatial — each comes from where that person stands in the scene — with a stereo toggle, per-person mute and a speaking indicator in the panel. Audio goes browser to browser; it never passes through Verse's server.

Switching apps: Android phones and desktops keep talking in the background. An iPhone pauses the microphone while you are in another app; when you come back, voice reconnects on its own. If the phone had to reload the page, voice comes back on too (if the browser asks again for the microphone, allow it, or tap the mic).

Phones on mobile data usually cannot reach each other directly, so voice uses a TURN relay when the server has one configured (VERSE_TURN_URLS plus either VERSE_TURN_SECRET for short-lived per-person credentials, or a provider's VERSE_TURN_USERNAME / VERSE_TURN_CREDENTIAL). Without a relay, voice still works between devices that can reach each other directly; the panel says so when a pair cannot connect.

Links and knobs#

  • /t/<code> → /view?vpk=<scene>&room=<room>&live=1 (a guest). ?room=<room>&host=1 hosts a room at once; a plain ?room= is the 2.7 viewer with the tour bar.
  • API: POST /v1/tour/invite, GET /v1/tour/invite/<code>, POST /v1/room/<room>/leave — api.md.
  • Server: VERSE_TOUR_INVITE_TTL_H (24) how long a link lasts; VERSE_TOUR_INVITES_PER_HOUR (60) invites per address per hour; VERSE_ROOM_AWAY_TTL_S (600) how long someone whose phone is in another app stays "away" before they count as gone.
  • ?prefetch=0 turns the background save off for one page.

Testing#

cd web/test && QA_PORT=8935 node fix-verify-tour-polish.mjs (ports 8930–8939) checks stepping away and coming back, reloads, the invite share round trip, the background save and voice across an app switch.

cd web/test && QA_PORT=10254 node fix-verify-tourlive.mjs (ports 10250–10299) runs a desktop host, two iPhone 13s and a WhatsApp in-app browser, each in its own Chromium. Without a GPU it runs on SwiftShader: expect several "GPU context recovered" device losses per run (none on real GPUs). The gate re-asserts the host's teleport after each one, and gives the follow checks a 40 s window because four software renderers share the CPU; on a real phone the glide lands in about a second. The pixels (pings drawn over the right object, the follow glide's smoothness) and real in-app browsers need a device check.

If you close the page for good, guests see "The agent left the tour" within a few seconds and keep their own cameras; the room stays open, so coming back on the same link puts you back in charge. Any guest can also take over with Host this tour in the tour bar.

Faster for late joiners. Once a tour starts, each phone quietly saves the rest of the home to its own storage in the background, so walking into a new room — or coming back after a break — does not wait on the network. It is skipped when the phone is in data-saver mode or on a slow connection, and it never takes more than a modest share of the phone's storage.

4. Hand over and end#
Hand over on a guest's row makes them the host; everyone follows them.
End tour gives everyone their own camera and shows "The tour has ended". Host again restarts it in the same room.
5. What is recorded#

Nothing from the tour is kept: poses live in memory for 10 s (10 minutes for someone who stepped away), names ride the roster only, the invite table holds {scene, room, expiry} and nothing else, and no audio or video exists. The one trace is analytics: a session that was part of a live tour counts as a live tour in the scene's analytics (Studio → Analytics shows Live tours beside views and enquiries; the CSV carries live_tour_sessions). The same privacy rules as the rest of analytics apply — no names, no addresses.

Voice#

Everyone in the tour can talk. Tap the round mic button on the tour chip (or Join voice in the panel); the browser asks for the microphone once. Then the mic shows its state at a glance:

green — your mic is on; it glows while you speak. Tap to mute.
red, crossed out — muted. Tap to unmute, or press and hold to talk just while you hold it (like a walkie-talkie), then let go.

Up to six people speak at a time; voices are spatial — each comes from where that person stands in the scene — with a stereo toggle, per-person mute and a speaking indicator in the panel. Audio goes browser to browser; it never passes through Verse's server.

Switching apps: Android phones and desktops keep talking in the background. An iPhone pauses the microphone while you are in another app; when you come back, voice reconnects on its own. If the phone had to reload the page, voice comes back on too (if the browser asks again for the microphone, allow it, or tap the mic).

Phones on mobile data usually cannot reach each other directly, so voice uses a TURN relay when the server has one configured (VERSE_TURN_URLS plus either VERSE_TURN_SECRET for short-lived per-person credentials, or a provider's VERSE_TURN_USERNAME / VERSE_TURN_CREDENTIAL). Without a relay, voice still works between devices that can reach each other directly; the panel says so when a pair cannot connect.

Links and knobs#
/t/<code> → /view?vpk=<scene>&room=<room>&live=1 (a guest). ?room=<room>&host=1 hosts a room at once; a plain ?room= is the 2.7 viewer with the tour bar.
API: POST /v1/tour/invite, GET /v1/tour/invite/<code>, POST /v1/room/<room>/leave — api.md.
Server: VERSE_TOUR_INVITE_TTL_H (24) how long a link lasts; VERSE_TOUR_INVITES_PER_HOUR (60) invites per address per hour; VERSE_ROOM_AWAY_TTL_S (600) how long someone whose phone is in another app stays "away" before they count as gone.
?prefetch=0 turns the background save off for one page.
Testing#

cd web/test && QA_PORT=8935 node fix-verify-tour-polish.mjs (ports 8930–8939) checks stepping away and coming back, reloads, the invite share round trip, the background save and voice across an app switch.

cd web/test && QA_PORT=10254 node fix-verify-tourlive.mjs (ports 10250–10299) runs a desktop host, two iPhone 13s and a WhatsApp in-app browser, each in its own Chromium. Without a GPU it runs on SwiftShader: expect several "GPU context recovered" device losses per run (none on real GPUs). The gate re-asserts the host's teleport after each one, and gives the follow checks a 40 s window because four software renderers share the CPU; on a real phone the glide lands in about a second. The pixels (pings drawn over the right object, the follow glide's smoothness) and real in-app browsers need a device check.

/guides/publish-from-unity.html:
How-to guides

Publish from Unity#

Status: verified on Unity 6000.6.5f1 (Apple silicon), 2026-10-13. A real editor imported a glTF model (glTFast 6.14.1, resolved automatically), exported a textured scene, ran the bundled verse-prepare, uploaded (one-shot and resumable), compiled and showed the link in the window; the link rendered textured. A dead server shows a plain-language error. Bake-on-publish v2 measured on Boat Attack (URP 17, terrain), a lightmapped URP interior and an HDRP room — see Measured.

A Tools ▸ Verse ▸ Publish Scene editor window exports the open scene (or the selection) to GLB with glTFast, uploads it, shows the server's compile stages live, and gives you a streaming link.

You need: Unity 2021.3 or newer (2022.3 LTS recommended). The package depends on com.unity.cloud.gltfast, pulled in automatically.

1. Install the package#

Download#

Download com.ctruh.verse-publish-3.0.0.tgz (3.0 MB) from the downloads page. It bundles verse-prepare for macOS (Apple silicon and Intel), Windows and Linux under Tools~/. Check it before installing:

shasum -a 256 com.ctruh.verse-publish-3.0.0.tgz   # Windows: Get-FileHash com.ctruh.verse-publish-3.0.0.tgz -Algorithm SHA256
# 24741c9d4736784af4ed7ac9240d928d90d6cefd8c773a92dfc48df55a4d8505

Keep the file somewhere stable (Unity references a tarball by path — the project's Packages/ folder is a good place), then **Window ▸ Package Manager ▸ + ▸ Add package from tarball…** and pick it.

Other routes#

From a git URL — Window ▸ Package Manager ▸ + ▸ Add package from git URL…:

https://github.com/ctruh/verse-engine.git?path=integrations/unity/com.ctruh.verse-publish

Or from a tarball:

cd integrations/unity && ./make_tarball.sh   # -> dist/com.ctruh.verse-publish-3.0.0.tgz

then + ▸ Add package from tarball…. A local checkout also works as a "com.ctruh.verse-publish": "file:/path/to/integrations/unity/com.ctruh.verse-publish" entry in Packages/manifest.json. Every route resolves glTFast from the Unity registry (6.14.1 on Unity 6) and finds the bundled verse-prepare wherever the package lives. The install must finish with no console errors.

2. Server and token#

Open Tools ▸ Verse ▸ Publish Scene. The window holds, persisted via EditorPrefs:

FieldWhat it does
Server URLPrefilled with the hosted service. Point it at your own origin when you run your own server.
Account tokenOptional, entered in a password field, sent as Authorization: Bearer. Owned scenes are permanent and listed in /studio; token uploads use the per-token rate bucket (20/hour). Leave empty for an anonymous test.

3. Publish#

  1. Set the scene name (defaults to the active scene) or tick Selection only.
  2. Press Publish scene.

Progress runs export → upload % → Compiling — <stage> → done. The upload streams from disk (UploadHandlerFile, HTTP/1.1), the compile stage is the server's live text passed through verbatim, polling runs on EditorApplication.update so the editor never blocks, and Cancel works in every phase. On success the link is shown, auto-copied, and Copy link / Open in browser are offered.

Server errors are shown verbatim. The window retries exactly once, and only on failures that lack the X-Verse-Error header (edge/proxy failures) — an application error is final and actionable.

If the server cannot be reached at all (wrong URL, server down, no network) the window says so in plain words — "Could not reach the Verse server at <host>. Check the Server URL above and your connection, then publish again." — instead of a transport error.

Publish from a script or CI#

The same state machine runs without the window:

Unity -batchmode -projectPath <project> -logFile publish.log \
  -executeMethod Ctruh.VersePublish.VersePublishBatch.PublishFromCommandLine \
  -verseScene Assets/Scenes/Main.unity -verseServer https://verse.ctruh.com \
  -verseName my-scene -verseResult result.json \
  [-verseBake auto|on|off] [-verseBakeQuality draft|high] [-verseNoSky]

Do not pass -quit (the publish runs on the editor update loop and the method exits the editor itself: 0 on success, 1 on failure) or -nographics (glTFast reads textures back through the GPU). A token, if any, comes from the VERSE_TOKEN environment variable. Editor scripts can call VersePublishBatch.Publish(...) or VersePublishWindow.PublishHeadless(...) directly.

Bake materials & lighting (bake-on-publish)#

glTFast exports what it can read off Unity's standard Lit property names. Custom shaders, Shader Graphs, detail/layered materials and all of Unity's baked lighting (lightmaps, light probes) are lost, so scenes arrive flat and grey. The window's Bake materials & lighting option bakes what the Game view shows, in the editor, right before the export:

Window setting
Bake materials & lighting: Auto / On / OffAuto is on for scenes (lightmaps present, a Terrain, 6+ renderers, 2+ lights or ≥ 3 m across) and off for a single product; the window says which it chose.
Quality: Draft / HighDraft: up to 8 bake pages of 2048² (64 texels/m near the camera), 1K material captures, a 4K sun shadow map, terrain from every second height sample. High: up to 24 pages (192 texels/m), 2K captures, 8K shadows, terrain at full resolution.
Sky as backgroundOn by default — see Terrain, LODs and the sky.

What a bake page holds. Every opaque, cut-out and blended renderer is rasterised into a rectangle of a few 2048² bake pages in its own lightmap UV layout (Unity's TEXCOORD1 unwrap — TEXCOORD0 when a lightmapped mesh has no second UV set, as Unity does; generated with Unwrapping for a dynamic mesh without one). Each texel is what Unity shows there:

  • surface — the renderer's material drawn through its own Meta pass (the pass Unity's lightmapper reads albedo and emission from; Standard, URP Lit, HDRP Lit, surface shaders and Shader Graph Lit all have one) straight into the page, with the mesh's real world normals and positions, so tiling, detail layers, triplanar projection, moss on upward faces and procedural maths come out as they look. Materials without a Meta pass use main texture × colour.
  • × indirect light — the renderer's lightmap (read as raw HDR from a temporary uncompressed re-import of its EXR, so the platform encoding is never guessed; directional lightmaps applied with the surface normal), or for a dynamic renderer its light probe as full L2 spherical harmonics per texel.
  • + direct light the lightmap does not hold — Realtime lights and Mixed lights in Baked Indirect or Shadowmask mode (a Subtractive lightmap already holds its Mixed lights): each light's diffuse term with its own falloff and spot cone, normal maps included, shadowed from a shadow map rendered for the bake (directional: one orthographic map over the scene; spot: one perspective map; point: six cube faces). Fully Baked lights are in the lightmap and the probes already.
  • + emission, all of it encoded through the **editor camera's colour grading**: a URP camera that renders post-processing is read once per publish as a 3D LUT (an identity colour cube drawn on a quad through a copy of the camera — Unity's own post exposure, white balance, lift/gamma/gain, curves and tonemapping), so the link shows the graded look, not the raw radiance.

Renderers are paged by place (Z-order of their positions) and packed by size, at a texel density chosen from the quality, the object's surface and its distance from the main camera (full density within ~30 m, a third far away), scaled to the page budget. A level with 900 objects compiles 7–20 textures instead of one per object (Boat Attack High: 512 s of server compile before, 32 s now). The pages are exported as emissive-only VersePage<n>_Baked materials on mesh copies whose first UV set addresses the page — the shape Verse's compiler detects as a bake and shows unlit — and the link opens with auto=0, so Verse's first-open auto exposure does not re-expose an already graded image.

Cut-outs keep their holes. A material whose Meta pass clips (an alpha-clipped Shader Graph, URP/HDRP Lit with alpha clipping) is detected from the capture's coverage; one that does not clip but is declared cut-out takes main texture alpha × colour alpha. The holes travel in the page's own alpha (Verse reads a cut-out's alpha in the same UV set as its baked colour), cut-outs get twice the texel density, and they export as glTF MASK (blended materials as BLEND). Baked cut-out geometry goes out in primitives of under 128 triangles: Verse builds a far-distance impostor for every alpha-cut primitive above that, whose atlas is lit, not baked — on a level with 300 trees that cost ~80 s of compile and made the scene stop reading as a bake.

Skinned meshes keep one colour per object (albedo × probe light + the average sun). Lights are not exported once the lighting is baked in.

Nothing in your scene changes. Renderer materials, meshes and enabled flags are swapped for the export and restored afterwards (also on error or Cancel); the temporary lightmap copy is deleted. The window shows Baking materials 4 / 13, Preparing meshes 64 / 920, Shadows: Sun…, Baking page 2 / 7 and, when done, what the bake did. Batch mode: -verseBake auto|on|off -verseBakeQuality draft|high [-verseNoSky]; the result JSON carries bake (pages, objects, cut-outs, direct lights, per-phase seconds) and scene (LOD, terrain, sky, grade) objects.

Terrain, LODs and the sky#

These run on every publish, bake on or off:

  • LOD groups go out as LOD0 only (glTFast exported every level on top of each other — z-fighting, 2–4× the triangles, and the coarse levels had no lightmap). Verse builds its own LOD chain.
  • Terrain becomes tile meshes of ~64 m (heightmap sampled at every second sample on Draft, every sample on High), its splat layers composited on the GPU into one base-colour and one normal texture per terrain (layer tiling, offset and tint included). The tiles carry the terrain's lightmap, so the bake treats them like any lightmapped object; the terrain's trees become instances of their prototypes (up to 4,000). Detail meshes and grass are not exported.
  • Sky and background. The skybox (whatever draws it — procedural, 6-sided, cubemap or a custom sky shader) is rendered into a cubemap from the main camera and unwrapped to an equirect, graded like the bake. An account-owned publish (token set) uploads it as the scene's Radiance .hdr background (PUT /v1/scenes/<id>/background/image): every visitor sees the sky, and it lights the live-lit parts of the scene. An anonymous publish cannot set a background, so the link carries it: bg=grad:<above>,<horizon>, on live-lit and baked scenes alike (since 3.0.0 Verse shows gradients behind baked scenes and paints solid colours exactly).

Measured#

Unity 6000.6.5f1 (Apple silicon), local server with empty caches, 2026-10-13 — ΔE2000 between a camera render in the editor and the published Verse link from the same pose (mean over the frame; lower is closer; integrations/bake-proof/unity/compare-unity.mjs), publish = click to link:

SceneBake offDraftHigh
Boat Attack demo_Island (URP 17, 2 terrains, 920 renderers after LOD0, Shader Graph cliffs and vegetation, Mixed sun in Baked Indirect, colour-graded camera)ΔE 17.9 · 35.5 sΔE 10.0 · 21.3 s (bake 2.2 s, 7 pages)ΔE 9.9 · 41.8 s (bake 5.3 s, 20 pages)
URP interior (window, Mixed sun + Mixed spot in Baked Indirect, baked lamp, cut-out plant and perforated screen, detail-mapped rug, probe-lit vase, procedural sky)ΔE 18.2 · 1.8 sΔE 4.7 · 5.2 sΔE 4.6 · 6.9 s
The same room under HDRP 17 (fixed exposure, gradient sky)ΔE 15.6 · 1.6 sΔE 8.7 · 4.2 sΔE 8.6 · 5.9 s

Before this version Boat Attack measured ΔE 29.0 (off), 32.0 (Draft, 44 s) and 32.0 (High, 900 s); the "off" column improves too because the terrain, LOD0 and the sky now travel on every publish. Draft is faster than a plain publish on Boat Attack: seven 2048² pages compile faster than the level's own twelve source textures (two of them 4K). Side-by-sides: Verse-Bake-On-Publish-Proof/unity-v2/ (*.sheet.png: editor, off, Draft, High).

Limits. Boat Attack's sea is drawn by a script at run time — there is no mesh to export, so the link has no water. A baked scene's background is one colour (a gradient or the sky image needs a token). HDRP: the camera's exposure and tonemapping are not read (the bake's direct light in the HDRP room is too bright by about that factor). Fine alpha patterns (a perforated screen) close up at the page's resolution. World-space shaders on cut-out materials use their one-tile capture. Bloom, vignette and depth of field are not carried. Skinned meshes are one colour. Specular highlights are not baked (Verse's own reflections apply).

The prepare step (2.3)#

Between export and upload the plug-in runs verse-prepare on the GLB: textures are right-sized to the texel density the scene can show (default 2048 px/m — one texel per screen pixel at arm's length), opaque base colour goes to JPEG 92 (everything else stays lossless), duplicate meshes are instanced and unreferenced data is dropped. The panel shows the tool's own progress and result. Prepared files may be up to 20 GB; without the tool, exports under 512 MB upload as they are (the server prepares them losslessly) and larger ones stop with the install hint. Preferences: prepare on/off, the binary path, texels per metre, lossless. Details, flags and how the binaries are bundled: verse-prepare.

What gets exported#

  • GLB via glTFast 6.x, textures at source resolution (never downscaled — bake at the quality you want published); bake pages as JPEG 92 (PNG where they carry cut-out alpha).
  • LOD0 of every LOD group, Terrains as tile meshes, the skybox as the background — on every publish.
  • The protocol layer (VersePublishClient.cs) is plain C# with no UnityEngine dependency, so the same request shapes are replayed by the headless test.
  • 30-minute total budget, matching one server compile attempt (30 min; a build's whole wall clock is 45 min).

Known seams to watch#

  • glTFast export API drift on future glTFast majors (errors mentioning GameObjectExport or ExportSettings) — 6.14.1 works as-is.
  • Textures arriving downscaled — they must be source resolution.

Next#

  • Share privately with tokens
  • Embed the viewer
  • Publish from Unreal

Unity 6000.6.5f1 (Apple silicon), local server with empty caches, 2026-10-13 — ΔE2000 between a camera render in the editor and the published Verse link from the same pose (mean over the frame; lower is closer; integrations/bake-proof/unity/compare-unity.mjs), publish = click to link:

Scene	Bake off	Draft	High
Boat Attack demo_Island (URP 17, 2 terrains, 920 renderers after LOD0, Shader Graph cliffs and vegetation, Mixed sun in Baked Indirect, colour-graded camera)	ΔE 17.9 · 35.5 s	ΔE 10.0 · 21.3 s (bake 2.2 s, 7 pages)	ΔE 9.9 · 41.8 s (bake 5.3 s, 20 pages)
URP interior (window, Mixed sun + Mixed spot in Baked Indirect, baked lamp, cut-out plant and perforated screen, detail-mapped rug, probe-lit vase, procedural sky)	ΔE 18.2 · 1.8 s	ΔE 4.7 · 5.2 s	ΔE 4.6 · 6.9 s
The same room under HDRP 17 (fixed exposure, gradient sky)	ΔE 15.6 · 1.6 s	ΔE 8.7 · 4.2 s	ΔE 8.6 · 5.9 s

Before this version Boat Attack measured ΔE 29.0 (off), 32.0 (Draft, 44 s) and 32.0 (High, 900 s); the "off" column improves too because the terrain, LOD0 and the sky now travel on every publish. Draft is faster than a plain publish on Boat Attack: seven 2048² pages compile faster than the level's own twelve source textures (two of them 4K). Side-by-sides: Verse-Bake-On-Publish-Proof/unity-v2/ (*.sheet.png: editor, off, Draft, High).

Limits. Boat Attack's sea is drawn by a script at run time — there is no mesh to export, so the link has no water. A baked scene's background is one colour (a gradient or the sky image needs a token). HDRP: the camera's exposure and tonemapping are not read (the bake's direct light in the HDRP room is too bright by about that factor). Fine alpha patterns (a perforated screen) close up at the page's resolution. World-space shaders on cut-out materials use their one-tile capture. Bloom, vignette and depth of field are not carried. Skinned meshes are one colour. Specular highlights are not baked (Verse's own reflections apply).

The prepare step (2.3)#

Between export and upload the plug-in runs verse-prepare on the GLB: textures are right-sized to the texel density the scene can show (default 2048 px/m — one texel per screen pixel at arm's length), opaque base colour goes to JPEG 92 (everything else stays lossless), duplicate meshes are instanced and unreferenced data is dropped. The panel shows the tool's own progress and result. Prepared files may be up to 20 GB; without the tool, exports under 512 MB upload as they are (the server prepares them losslessly) and larger ones stop with the install hint. Preferences: prepare on/off, the binary path, texels per metre, lossless. Details, flags and how the binaries are bundled: verse-prepare.

What gets exported#
GLB via glTFast 6.x, textures at source resolution (never downscaled — bake at the quality you want published); bake pages as JPEG 92 (PNG where they carry cut-out alpha).
LOD0 of every LOD group, Terrains as tile meshes, the skybox as the background — on every publish.
The protocol layer (VersePublishClient.cs) is plain C# with no UnityEngine dependency, so the same request shapes are replayed by the headless test.
30-minute total budget, matching one server compile attempt (30 min; a build's whole wall clock is 45 min).
Known seams to watch#
glTFast export API drift on future glTFast majors (errors mentioning GameObjectExport or ExportSettings) — 6.14.1 works as-is.
Textures arriving downscaled — they must be source resolution.
Next#
Share privately with tokens
Embed the viewer
Publish from Unreal
